text: The symbol with several bumps means uneven road: it warns that the road surface is irregular.
The uneven road sign warns that the roadway may be damaged or in poor condition.
The red-bordered triangle warns of a hazard: here, an uneven road.
The sign indicates an uneven road, not a steep descent: it warns of an irregular surface.
The bumps represent an uneven road surface; dangerous bends have a different sign.
The symbol indicates an uneven road; a double bend has a different sign.
The uneven surface can make vehicles coming from the opposite direction harder to control too, so anticipate possible deviations.
The sign warns of an uneven surface: slowing down helps you maintain control.
On an uneven surface, jolts can affect steering: a firm but relaxed grip helps you control the handlebars.
An uneven surface calls for an appropriate, cautious speed, not an increase in speed.
Do not reduce the gap: leave enough room to stop without hitting the vehicle ahead.
The sign warns of an uneven surface and does not require you to stop for every oncoming vehicle; proceed cautiously.
The hill crest sign is a warning sign: it is normally placed 150 metres before the hazard.
A crest is a convex change in the road that can hide what lies beyond its top.
A crest is an uphill section followed by a descent: its top restricts your view of the road beyond.
The single hump indicates a crest that limits visibility; an uneven road has a different symbol.
This is the crest sign, indicating a convex change in the road; it does not mean the surface is damaged.
The symbol indicates a crest with limited visibility; roadworks have a different sign.
The crest restricts your view: slow down so you can stop within the distance you can see.
Visibility is limited at a crest, where making a U-turn is prohibited.
Visibility is limited at a crest, so a stopped vehicle may be seen too late. Stopping and parking are prohibited on the crest, both uphill and downhill.
The sign warns of a crest and does not require you to drive in the centre: normally, drive on the right near the edge.
The sign indicates a crest that restricts visibility, not a damaged surface; adapt your driving to what you can see.
Parking is also prohibited on the uphill section of the crest: limited visibility may prevent other drivers from seeing the parked vehicle in time.
The symbol with a concave profile indicates a dip, a depression in the road.
The concave profile in the triangle marks a dip: the road descends and then rises, forming a hollow.
A dip is a hollow in the road profile: a descent is followed by a climb.
The concave symbol warns of a dip; an uneven road surface has a different sign.
The symbol marks a dip, a hollow in the road; it does not warn that the carriageway narrows.
The concave profile indicates a dip; a hill crest is a convex rise and has a different symbol.
A dip changes the road profile: slowing down helps keep the moped under control while crossing it.
A dip calls for care; rain makes the road wet and reduces grip, making loss of control more likely.
Leaving more room to the vehicle ahead allows time to react and stop if it slows for the dip. Adjust the distance to road conditions.
The triangle warns of a dip; it does not require overtaking. Overtake only when conditions permit it.
The dip does not require overtaking: the maneuver requires enough clear space, taking oncoming vehicles into account.
For a dip, adjust and reduce speed to maintain control, rather than accelerating.
The symbol shows the road bending right and warns of a dangerous bend in that direction.
The dangerous right bend can limit the view along the road: approach it with the available visibility in mind.
The dangerous right bend calls for a speed suited to the road layout and visibility so that control is maintained.
The triangle warns of a dangerous right bend; it is not a prohibition on turning at a junction.
The sign warns of a dangerous right bend in the road, not a junction where turning is compulsory.
The symbol marks a dangerous right bend in the road, not a lane change.
The sign warns of a dangerous bend. A wet road reduces grip, so take extra care through it.
Near or on a bend, overtaking is prohibited on a road with one lane in each direction: it lacks the configuration required for the exception.
On a bend, adjust speed to visibility and geometry: a tighter bend requires a lower speed to maintain control.
Do not aim for the center line: keep to the right side of the carriageway, near its right edge, including on bends.
A dangerous bend calls for an appropriate speed and control; high speed can prevent you from following the path safely.
A U-turn is prohibited near or on a bend, where the maneuver can create danger.
The symbol shows the road bending left and warns of a dangerous bend in that direction.
The dangerous left bend can limit the view along the road: approach it with the available visibility in mind.
The triangle with a leftward bend warns of a dangerous bend; warning signs are normally placed 150 m before the danger.
The sign indicates a dangerous left bend, not an obstacle to pass on the left.
This warning sign announces a left bend; it does not prohibit a turn.
It warns of a left bend in the road, not a junction or a mandatory turn.
Read the symbol from the bottom: it shows two successive dangerous bends, the first to the right.
The triangle warns of a dangerous double bend, the first to the right; the usual distance is 150 m.
The double bend is dangerous: reduce speed and adapt it to road conditions.
The triangle warns of a double bend, the first to the right; it does not prohibit a turn.
The symbol indicates a dangerous double bend, not a descent.
The symbol indicates a dangerous double bend, not a slippery surface.
The double bend calls for attention to position: drive on the right side of the carriageway.
On bends, adapt speed to the road layout and visibility to retain control of the vehicle.

Overtaking near or on bends is prohibited in the usual case of a two-way carriageway with one lane in each direction. The code allows exceptions, including roads with separate carriageways and the required road markings.
The sign warns of dangerous bends: U-turns are prohibited near or on bends.
Adjust speed for both bends and visibility conditions, not just the first bend.
It is not always allowed: stopping and parking are prohibited on bends and, outside built-up areas and on urban through roads, also near them.
Read the symbol from the bottom: it shows two successive dangerous bends, the first to the left.
The triangle warns of a dangerous double bend, the first to the left; the usual distance is 150 m.
The double bend is dangerous: reduce speed and adapt it to road conditions.
The symbol warns of a double bend, the first to the left, not a narrowing.
The symbol warns of a double bend, the first to the left, not a slippery carriageway.
This is a warning sign for a double bend, the first to the left; it does not prohibit a turn.
The barrier symbol in the triangle warns of a railway crossing with full or half barriers.
The sign warns of a crossing with full or half barriers: at the crossing there may be one steady red light for full barriers or two alternately flashing red lights for half barriers.
The sign warns of a crossing with full or half barriers; an audible device may warn that they are closing.
The triangle with a barrier warns of a level crossing with barriers or half-barriers, not a dead-end road.
The triangle with a barrier warns of a protected level crossing; it does not require a diversion.
Closed half-barriers prohibit entering the crossing, even if there is space between the arms.
The sign warns of a protected level crossing: slow down and be ready to stop before closed barriers.
Flashing red lights mean you must not enter the level crossing: stop before it.
An active audible warning prohibits entering the level crossing: stop before the crossing.
Do not go around a closed half-barrier: entering the crossing is prohibited even if there is space between the arms.
Stopping and parking are prohibited on railway tracks and in their immediate vicinity: a stationary vehicle could obstruct a train.
Red-and-white barricades blocking the crossing prevent passage: they can replace barriers if those fail.
The triangle with a locomotive warns of a railway crossing without barriers; the sign for a crossing with barriers shows a barrier.
The sign warns of a level crossing without barriers: approach with particular care and check before crossing.
The triangle warns of the crossing without barriers; the St Andrew’s cross is normally placed near the tracks, after the warning sign.
The locomotive in the triangle indicates a level crossing without barriers, not a tram stop.
The locomotive warns of a level crossing without barriers; the sign for one with barriers shows a barrier.
The locomotive in the triangle warns of a railway crossing without barriers, not the presence of tram tracks.
As you approach a crossing without barriers, slow down so you can stop before the tracks if necessary.
At a crossing without barriers, check both directions along the railway: a train can come from the right or left.
Stopping and parking are prohibited on railway tracks and in their immediate vicinity, so as not to obstruct trains.
Slowing down is not limited to fog: a level crossing calls for caution and a moderate speed even in good visibility.
The triangle alone does not always require a stop: stop when signs, signals or an approaching train require it.
Do not cross when red-and-white barricades block the crossing: the barrier closes the route.
The St Andrew’s cross indicates the immediate vicinity of a railway crossing without barriers.
The cross is placed by the track at the crossing, rather than at the distance of the triangular warning sign.
First comes the triangular warning sign for a crossing without barriers; the cross is at the crossing.
The single cross shown indicates one track; a double cross is used for two or more tracks.
The cross marks a level crossing without barriers or half-barriers; any alternating red lights do not indicate the presence of half-barriers.
The cross may be accompanied by two alternating flashing red lights, not one green and one red light.
The double cross marks an unbarriered crossing with multiple tracks: if a train is approaching, stop before the stop line.
The double cross indicates two or more tracks; the single cross indicates one track.
The double cross indicates multiple tracks: after one train passes, another may arrive on a different track.
The double cross stands immediately near the tracks; the triangular advance warning sign is normally farther away.
The double cross indicates at least two tracks; a single cross is used for one track.
The double cross marks a crossing without barriers or half-barriers; a separate advance warning sign is used for half-barriers.
The panels accompany advance warnings of crossings with barriers or half-barriers and crossings without barriers.
In the usual arrangement, the three-bar panel is about 150 metres away; the two- and one-bar panels are at two thirds and one third of that distance, about 100 and 50 metres.
The bars decrease from three to one as you approach the crossing, indicating the progressively shorter distance.
The panels also accompany the advance warning of an unbarriered crossing, not only one with barriers or half-barriers.
These are distance panels for a level crossing: the bars indicate the approach to the railway, not roadworks.
The bars indicate the approach to the level crossing; they do not represent the number of tracks.
The triangle warns of a tram line that may cross or reduce the space available to other vehicles: allow for the space occupied by the tram.
The sign warns of a tram line: there may be passengers on foot at a stop, whose movement must not be obstructed.
The sign warns of a tram line. On tracks level with the road, vehicles may proceed only without obstructing or slowing the tram.

The triangle warns of a tram line and does not always prohibit overtaking: a tram not on reserved track may be passed on the right if the carriageway is wide enough, subject to the other safety conditions.

The sign does not itself prohibit driving on tracks level with the road: this is permitted if compatible with traffic needs, without obstructing or slowing the tram, and subject to any contrary signs.
Not always: if the tram is stopped in the middle of the carriageway for passengers to board or alight and there is no refuge island, passing it on the right is prohibited.
The triangle showing a pedestrian on stripes warns of a pedestrian crossing marked on the road.
The sign warns of a crossing: when traffic is not controlled by officers or traffic lights, drivers must stop for pedestrians using it.
Overtaking a vehicle stopped or slowed at a crossing to let pedestrians cross is prohibited: it may conceal them from view.
The triangle warns of a pedestrian crossing marked on the road, not an avenue reserved for pedestrians.
The sign warns of a crossing and does not require sounding the horn; the horn must be used only for safety and with moderation.
The sign warns of a pedestrian crossing: stopping and parking on it are forbidden even if space remains for pedestrians.
The stopped vehicle is letting pedestrians cross: overtaking it at the crossing is prohibited.
The sign warns of a crossing: slow down and be ready to stop to let pedestrians cross.
The crossing must remain clear: both stopping and parking on it are prohibited.
Pedestrians on the crossing do not automatically require a horn: slow down and yield; use the horn only for safety.
Not just for children: slow down approaching the crossing and let other pedestrians cross too.
At a crossing without traffic control, drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing or in its immediate vicinity.
The triangle with a cyclist warns of a marked cycle crossing where bicycles may cross the road.
This is a warning sign: it is normally placed 150 metres before the danger, here the cycle crossing.
Cyclists may use the crossing: adjust speed so as not to endanger them.
The triangle warns of bicycles before the crossing; it is not placed after every crossing.
The triangle warns of a cycle crossing; it does not prohibit cyclists from passing.
The triangle warns of a place where cyclists cross the road, not the beginning of a cycle path.
The sign warns that bicycles may cross: adjust speed to avoid endangering cyclists.
At a cycle crossing drivers must yield to cyclists: slow down and be ready to stop to let them pass.
The vehicle ahead has stopped to let cyclists cross: wait too, since overtaking it would obstruct their crossing.
Do not sound the horn automatically when cyclists are present: let them cross and use the horn only for safety.
At a cycle crossing drivers must yield to cyclists, not the other way around.
Priority at a cycle crossing is not limited to cyclists coming from the right: let cyclists from the other side pass too.
The triangle with a downward slope warns of a dangerous descent; the number indicates the gradient.
Stopping distance increases downhill: leave more space from the vehicle ahead so you can stop safely.
The sign warns of a steep descent: moderate your speed to retain control.
The symbol indicates a dangerous descent, not an uneven road surface: the warning concerns the slope.
The indicated gradient is downhill: the profile slopes down to the right and does not represent an ascent.
The profile slopes down to the right: the sign warns of a dangerous descent, not an ascent.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Moderate your speed to keep control, as a vehicle tends to accelerate downhill.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Excessive, prolonged use of the brakes can overheat them and reduce their effectiveness.
Stopping downhill may take more space. Increasing the gap to the vehicle ahead leaves more room to stop.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. On a wet road, reduced grip makes braking more difficult and calls for particular care.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Other conditions being equal, the slope works against braking, so braking distance increases rather than decreases.
Stopping downhill may take more space, so increase the gap to the vehicle ahead rather than reducing it.
The black triangle rises to the right: this is the steep uphill sign, placed before a dangerous ascending stretch.
The steep uphill sign warns of an ascending stretch whose gradient, together with local conditions, can create danger.
The triangle indicates a steep uphill stretch, and 10% expresses its gradient, not its length.
The sign indicates a steep ascent, not a descent. The uphill slope opposes motion and does not by itself increase braking distance.
The triangle marked 10% indicates a steep ascent; dangerous bends have signs with different symbols.
The sign indicates a steep ascent, not a descent; 10% expresses the uphill gradient.
The two converging lines indicate a symmetrical narrowing: the carriageway narrows on both sides.
At a symmetrical narrowing the carriageway is narrower, so passing oncoming vehicles can become difficult.
The narrowing leaves less space. Moderate your speed to pass possible oncoming traffic safely.
The sign warns of a symmetrical narrowing; by itself it does not give priority over oncoming vehicles.
The lines move closer together: they indicate a symmetrical narrowing of the carriageway, not a widening.
The lines indicate a symmetrical narrowing of the carriageway; the sign does not indicate a tunnel.
The left line moves towards the centre while the right line stays straight: the road narrows on the left.
The narrowing on the left reduces the available space and can make passing oncoming traffic difficult.
The narrowing on the left leaves less room to pass. Slow down and, if necessary to let traffic pass, stop.
The line moving towards the centre indicates a narrowing on the left, not a road joining from the left.
The symbol indicates a narrowing on the left side of the carriageway, not an overpass.
In the symbol the left line moves towards the centre: the narrowing is on the left, not the right.
The right line moves towards the centre: the sign warns of a dangerous narrowing on the right.
The sign warns of an asymmetric narrowing on the right: the carriageway narrows on that side, possibly because of a low wall or another obstacle.
The sign warns of narrowing on the right; it does not indicate how many directions traffic travels in and can also be used on a two-way carriageway.
The sign warns of a narrowing on the right of the carriageway, not the end of two-way traffic.
The sign warns of narrowing on the right; on its own it does not mean that traffic must always alternate through the narrow section.
The sign warns of a narrowing on the right, not the start of a one-way road.
The sign warns of a section that may be more slippery than usual in certain conditions; panels specify those conditions, such as rain.
The surface can become unusually slippery: adjust and reduce speed to suit the road conditions and retain control.
On a slippery surface, moderate your speed and avoid sudden manoeuvres, which can cause a skid.
The skidding-car symbol warns of a slippery road; a narrowing has a different sign.
A slippery road can require more distance to stop, not less: reduced grip makes braking more difficult.
On a slippery road increase, rather than reduce, the distance from the vehicle ahead, because the distance needed to stop can increase.
The sign warns that the carriageway can become more slippery, so speed must be adjusted to the actual conditions.
Rain can make the surface slippery: slowing down and braking smoothly help prevent a skid.
Rain can make the surface slippery: slowing down and avoiding sudden steering help maintain control.
In rain braking distance can increase, not decrease, because grip on a wet surface is reduced.
In rain increase, rather than decrease, the distance from the vehicle ahead: more room may be needed to stop on a wet road.
Sudden acceleration on a wet road can cause a skid. Instead, moderate your speed and use the controls smoothly.
The children warning sign indicates places they frequent, such as schools, public gardens and playgrounds.
A school is one of the places frequented by children that the sign can warn about: it signals their possible presence nearby.
The sign warns of a place frequented by children: watch for their possible presence and adjust your speed.
The triangle warns of a place frequented by children; it does not prohibit U-turns.
The sign warns of a place frequented by children, not the end of an avenue reserved for them.
The sign warns that children may be present; by itself it does not prohibit motor vehicles from passing when school ends.
Children on the pavement may suddenly enter the carriageway: slow down near the indicated place and watch their movements.
Children can move suddenly and enter the carriageway: the sign calls for particular attention and an appropriate speed.
The sign warns of places frequented by children. A vehicle stopped to let them cross may hide them: overtaking it would put them in danger.
The sign warns of places frequented by children: even children on the sidewalk may enter the road.
The triangle warns of children; it does not by itself prohibit parking. Any parking restrictions applicable at the location still apply.
The sign warns that children may be present; it does not prohibit traffic when school ends. Adjust your speed and stop if necessary.
The opposing arrows warn that, after a one-way section, traffic will travel in both directions on the same carriageway.
The opposing arrows indicate a two-way section: vehicles may approach from the opposite direction on the same carriageway.
The triangle warns of a change from one-way to two-way traffic on the same carriageway, so the one-way section ends.
The two opposing arrows warn of two-way traffic, not the start of one-way traffic.
The triangle warns of two-way traffic; by itself it does not give oncoming vehicles priority.
The arrows represent the two directions of traffic on the same carriageway, not an obligation to turn back.
The sign indicates loose material on the road, which may reduce grip and cause skidding.
Passing vehicles may throw loose material into the air: take care to avoid hitting pedestrians too.
The sign warns of gravel, crushed stone or other small loose material already on the road surface.
The sign warns of loose material; it does not require driving in the middle of the road.
Loose material can reduce grip: accelerating is not the remedy. Adjust your speed to the road conditions.
The vehicle throwing stones indicates loose material on the road. Falling rocks are indicated by the triangle showing a rock face.
The rock face with falling stones indicates a risk of rocks falling from the slope.
The sign warns both of possible falling stones and of stones that may already be on the carriageway.
Rocks may already have fallen onto the carriageway: slowing down helps you see them and stop in time.
The rock face and stones indicate falling rocks or rocks on the road; they do not indicate a slippery surface.
The sign warns of falling rocks or rocks on the road; it does not advise flashing headlights.
The symbol indicates falling rocks and possible stones on the carriageway, not that the road lacks asphalt.
The triangle with three discs warns of traffic lights ahead: prepare to obey their signals.
On the warning sign, the yellow disc may be replaced by a flashing yellow light; this refers to the sign itself.
The sign warns of traffic lights: adjusting speed allows you to stop if the light requires it.
The triangle with three lights warns of traffic signals ahead, not an unprotected railway crossing.
The symbol warns of traffic signals, not a level crossing with half-barriers, which has its own signs.
The symbol with three lights warns of traffic signals ahead; it is not an advance STOP warning.
The windsock warns of a stretch where strong crosswind gusts can push a vehicle sideways.
The windsock warns that strong crosswind gusts may strike a vehicle suddenly.
Crosswinds can push a vehicle off course: proceeding carefully and holding the handlebars firmly helps maintain control.
The windsock warns of possible crosswind gusts; low-flying aircraft are indicated by a different sign.
The windsock warns of possible crosswind gusts, not of an airport nearby.
The windsock warns of possible crosswind gusts, not of a tunnel entrance.
On exposed viaducts crosswind gusts can strike a vehicle and push it off course.
Crosswind gusts can push a vehicle sideways and cause it to swerve.
On leaving a tunnel, a vehicle passes from shelter into an exposed stretch and can be hit by crosswind gusts.
Wind can push vehicles off course: when overtaking, keep an adequate lateral distance rather than moving closer.
The sign warns of crosswinds but does not itself impose a general overtaking ban. The maneuver must still be possible without danger.
The sign warns of possible crosswind gusts; it does not require every vehicle to stop. Adapt your driving to the conditions.
The car at the crumbling edge indicates a dangerous shoulder that may not support the vehicle.
The sign warns that, when approaching the edge of the road, you could fall into a deep gutter or ditch.
The symbol indicates a dangerous, unstable or unusable shoulder: approaching the edge can be risky.
The triangle warns of a dangerous shoulder; it does not prohibit using the road.
The triangle warns of a dangerous shoulder, not a parking area.
The symbol indicates a dangerous or unstable shoulder, not loose gravel on the roadway.
The yellow triangle with a worker signals roadworks and draws attention to the work.
The yellow triangle with a worker is the roadworks sign, placed near road work sites.
The roadworks sign warns of a work site where workers may be on the road.
The roadworks sign warns of a work site; by itself it does not require a stop. Follow any additional signs or instructions.
This is a roadworks sign: it warns of a work site, not an obligation to give way to oncoming traffic.
This is a roadworks sign: it warns of a work site and does not require you to turn around.
The white disc with a red border means no vehicles: the road is closed to vehicles in both directions.
The plain white disc with a red border means no traffic: all vehicles are prohibited in both directions.
The no-vehicles sign applies to all vehicles, including mopeds.
This sign prohibits vehicles in both directions. The no-entry sign, with a white bar on red, prohibits entry from the side where it is placed.
The white disc with a red border prohibits vehicles in both directions; it does not indicate a one-way road.
The no-vehicles sign applies to all vehicles, including motorised quadricycles.
The white bar on red means no entry: it prevents entry from that side into a road used in the opposite direction.
The no-entry sign applies to all vehicles, including motorised tricycles and quadricycles.
The no-entry sign prevents vehicles, including bicycles, from entering from the side where it is placed.
The no-entry sign bars vehicles generally from entering on the side where it is placed, so mopeds are included too.
The no-entry sign prevents entry from that side; it marks the exit end of a one-way road, not a two-way road.
The white bar on red means no entry and prevents entry from that side; the no-overtaking sign shows two vehicles.
The no-overtaking sign excludes mopeds from the motor vehicles that cannot be overtaken. The other conditions for the manoeuvre still apply.
The no-overtaking sign excludes motorcycles from the motor vehicles that cannot be overtaken. The other conditions for the manoeuvre still apply.
Mopeds are excluded from the motor vehicles this sign prohibits overtaking. The manoeuvre remains subject to the other applicable conditions.
The prohibition does not cover every vehicle: for example, mopeds and motorcycles are excluded. The manoeuvre remains subject to the other applicable conditions.
The sign with two vehicles means no overtaking; it does not reserve a lane for slow vehicles.
The prohibition also applies to a moped rider: a car is among the motor vehicles that cannot be overtaken.
The number in the disc is the maximum speed, here 80 km/h, which must not be exceeded on the affected stretch.
The red-bordered disc indicates a maximum speed of 80 km/h; lower limits may apply to some categories.
The value 80 is the maximum speed in km/h on the affected stretch, subject to any lower limits for certain categories.
The maximum of 80 km/h applies to vehicles generally, not just two-wheeled vehicles; some categories may have lower limits.
The red-bordered disc indicates a maximum speed of 80 km/h, not a minimum speed.
The number 80 indicates a maximum speed of 80 km/h; it is not a no-overtaking sign.
The crossed-out horn prohibits audible warnings, except in immediate danger.
The prohibition on using the horn has an exception for immediate danger.
The crossed-out horn marks the start of the prohibition on audible warnings, except in immediate danger.
The crossed-out horn prohibits its use: attracting attention is not a general permission; the immediate-danger exception remains.
The prohibition on audible warnings is not limited to night: the sign shown indicates no time restriction.
The crossed-out horn prohibits audible warnings, except in immediate danger; it does not require sounding the horn when meeting other vehicles.
The pedestrian inside the red circle indicates no entry for pedestrians.
The sign prohibits pedestrians from passing; it does not prohibit mopeds.
The sign prohibits pedestrians from passing; it does not prohibit motor quadricycles.
The sign prohibits pedestrians from passing and is not limited to 8:00–20:00: a supplementary panel can indicate a time restriction.
The sign prohibits pedestrians from using the road concerned; it does not indicate which edge to walk on.
The figure inside the red circle prohibits pedestrians from passing; it is not a sign requiring drivers to give way to them.
The motorcyclist inside the red circle indicates no entry for motorcycles.
The prohibition concerns motorcycles, not motor quadricycles, which are a separate category.
The prohibition concerns motorcycles; mopeds are a separate category and are not prohibited by this sign.
The prohibition concerns motorcycles, not all two-wheeled vehicles: for example, it does not prohibit bicycles.
The sign prohibits motorcycles even if the rider wears a helmet.
The sign prohibits motorcycles; it does not prohibit bicycles.
The bicycle symbol prohibits cycles; mopeds are a separate category.
The bicycle symbol prohibits cycles, not pedestrians.
The bicycle inside the red circle indicates no entry for cycles.
The prohibition on bicycles does not end at night: the sign shown indicates no time restriction.
The bicycle symbol prohibits cycles, not motorcycles.
The bicycle symbol prohibits cycles, not mopeds.

The car symbol prohibits Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as cars and trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles. It does not prohibit two-wheeled motorcycles or mopeds.

The prohibition covers Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as cars and trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles. Two-wheeled mopeds are not prohibited by this sign.

The prohibition covers Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as cars and trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles. Motorcycles are two-wheeled vehicles in the separate motoveicoli category and are not prohibited by this sign.

The sign prohibits Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as cars and trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles, from passing; it does not regulate parking.

The prohibition covers more than passenger cars: it extends to other Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles.

The sign prohibits Italian autoveicoli (motor vehicles with at least four wheels, excluding the separate motoveicoli category, which includes two- and three-wheeled motor vehicles and certain motor quadricycles), such as cars and trucks, as well as three-wheeled vehicles in the motoveicoli category and motor quadricycles, from passing; it does not identify a road reserved for pedestrians.
The black bar without other symbols identifies the end of restrictions: previously indicated restrictions cease at this point.
The diagonal black bar on a plain white circle identifies the end-of-restrictions sign: previously indicated prohibitions cease at that point.
The diagonal black bar on a plain white circle identifies the end-of-restrictions sign: previously indicated restrictions cease at that point.
The sign ends previously indicated restrictions; it is not limited to public service vehicles.
The black bar on white means the end of previous restrictions, not the end of a built-up area.
The sign means the end of previous restrictions, not the end of a slippery section of road.
The bar across the number ends the indicated speed restriction, and therefore that specific requirement.
The crossed-out 50 ends the posted 50 km/h maximum; the general limits for the road apply again.
The bar across 50 ends the corresponding maximum speed limit, meaning the prohibition on exceeding it.
The crossed-out 50 ends the posted limit; it does not impose a 50 km/h limit on all vehicles.
The crossed-out 50 ends the posted 50 km/h maximum speed limit, not a minimum distance between vehicles.
The crossed-out 50 ends the maximum speed limit; it does not prescribe a lane for slower vehicles.
The two crossed-out cars indicate the end of the previously imposed overtaking prohibition.
The sign ends the overtaking prohibition, but does not authorize crossing a solid longitudinal line to overtake.
The two crossed-out cars mark the point where the overtaking prohibition ends.
The sign ends the overtaking prohibition for all vehicles, not only between passenger cars.
The two crossed-out cars indicate the end of the overtaking prohibition, not a prohibition on passage.
The two crossed-out cars end the overtaking prohibition; the end of a speed limit uses a sign with a crossed-out number.
The overtaking prohibition excludes mopeds from its scope: a two-wheeled moped may therefore be overtaken if the maneuver complies with the other rules.
The overtaking ban does not cover motorcycles. The other overtaking rules still apply.
Bicycles are not motor vehicles, so this sign does not prohibit overtaking them. The other overtaking rules still apply.
The ban covers motor vehicles, with exceptions for mopeds and motorcycles. Electric propulsion does not exempt the category that includes cars, buses and trucks.
The sign sets no 40 km/h threshold: it excludes mopeds and motorcycles from the ban and does not prohibit overtaking non-motor vehicles.
Slow speed alone does not exempt a motor quadricycle: the sign provides exceptions for mopeds and motorcycles, not for slow vehicles as such.
A single diagonal bar means no parking. It does not itself prohibit a brief stop for a short-lived need.
This is a no-parking sign. On urban roads, without supplementary indications, it applies from 8:00 to 20:00.
This ban is not zonal: the sign must be repeated after an intersection for the ban to continue.

The arrow shows the one-way direction on the road concerned: traffic on it must follow that direction.
The arrow shows the one-way direction of the intersecting road; it does not require the viewer to turn left.
The arrows show the one-way direction on the respective roads; they do not require a driver seeing the sign to turn.
Each sign shows the one-way direction of the road it refers to; the pair does not prohibit turning in both directions.
The striped panel with an arrow identifies a roadworks vehicle exposed to traffic, whether stationary or moving.
The arrow shows the side on which to pass the works vehicle: in this figure, pass on the right.

This is not a roundabout sign: the panel marks a works vehicle and the arrow shows the side to pass on, here the right.
It does not require a right turn: the arrow directs traffic to pass to the right of the works vehicle carrying it.
The arrow points right: pass the marked vehicle or obstacle on that side, not on the left.
The sign marks the start of a pedestrian area. Bicycles and vehicles on emergency duty are generally also allowed, subject to any additional restrictions indicated.
The sign marks a pedestrian area and the panel below specifies the exceptions and access conditions.
The panel includes vehicles loading or unloading goods among the exceptions, under the conditions shown on it.
The sign marks the start of a pedestrian area; it is not a residential-zone sign.
The pedestrian symbol and wording indicate a pedestrian area, not a cycle track, although bicycles may be allowed there.
Vehicles are barred from the pedestrian area except for specified exceptions: the sign does not grant general access to mopeds.
The wording and disc mark the start of a limited traffic zone, with conditions specified on the panel.
The sign marks the start of a zone where access and circulation may be restricted by time or category.
A limited traffic zone may restrict circulation to particular categories; the panel specifies applicable exceptions.
The sign marks the start of a limited traffic zone, not an advance warning of a pedestrian area.
The wording and disc indicate a limited traffic zone, not a track reserved for bicycles.
The sign marks a limited traffic zone; it is not the sign prohibiting U-turns.
The square sign locates a pedestrian crossing without traffic lights; it is not the triangular advance warning sign.
The square sign is placed at the pedestrian crossing and identifies its location.
The sign marks a pedestrian crossing: slow down and stop if necessary to give pedestrians priority.
The sign marks where pedestrians cross the roadway; it does not give advance warning of a pedestrian avenue.
The sign marks a pedestrian crossing; it does not require sounding the horn. Use the horn only as permitted by the rules.
The sign marks a crossing for pedestrians; it does not prohibit them from passing.
The car symbol on a blue background marks the start of a road reserved for motor vehicles, distinct from a motorway.
The car symbol on a blue background identifies a road reserved for motor vehicles: the sign is placed at its entrances and replaces prohibition signs for non-motorized vehicles.
The sign concerns a road reserved for motor vehicles, not a single lane reserved solely for cars.
The sign marks a road reserved for motor vehicles and does not ban all motor quadricycles as a category. Motorway traffic restrictions still apply, including those based on vehicle mass.
The sign identifies a road reserved for motor vehicles; it does not require them to travel in single file.
This is the cycle crossing sign: it marks where the cycle track crosses the roadway, also identified by specific road markings.
The sign marks a cycle crossing, which is also identified by the appropriate road markings.
At a cycle crossing, cyclists’ paths can intersect those of vehicles. Proceed carefully and adjust your speed so you can react safely.
The sign marks a cycle crossing; a different sign marks the start of a cycle track.
The sign marks a cycle crossing on the roadway, not an area closed to motor vehicles.
The sign indicates where a cycle track crosses the roadway, not its position beside the sidewalk.
The arrows represent lanes and the bus symbol identifies the reserved lane: the sign indicates how they are used.
The bus symbol on the right arrow identifies the lane reserved for urban public transport buses.
The two arrows on the left indicate lanes for normal traffic; the right lane is reserved for buses.
The symbol on the right lane indicates urban service buses; the sign alone does not indicate that taxis may also use the reserved lane.
The yellow line separates the bus lane from the normal traffic lanes; it does not mark a cycle track.
The sign indicates the purpose and direction of the lanes; it does not always require travel in parallel lines.
A red light facing vehicles requires them to stop and not cross the stop line.
At a red light, stop without crossing the transverse stop line, leaving the intersection clear.
A red light requires stopping before the stop line, without entering the intersection.
A red light requires stopping before the stop line: caution alone does not permit a right turn.
A red light facing you requires you to stop: amber on the crossing road does not authorize you to move off. Wait for permission to proceed in your direction.
Red requires you to stop before the line; an empty junction does not allow you to cross it.
Green permits a left turn if signs and markings allow it, but you must yield to oncoming vehicles continuing across your path.
Green permits a turn allowed by signs and markings, but a turning driver must yield to pedestrians crossing with a simultaneous green signal.
Green allows travel in permitted directions, but approach cautiously and enter the junction only if you can clear it before red.
You need not wait for amber to turn: green permits the turn if signs and markings allow it, subject to priority rules. Amber warns of the need to stop.
A road need not be divided into lanes for a turn: on green you may follow a direction permitted by signs and markings, observing the rules for the maneuver.
Green gives permission to proceed in permitted directions; it does not always require stopping. Priority rules and the prohibition on blocking the junction still apply.
A green arrow permits vehicles to proceed in the direction it indicates, not in every direction.
A red arrow means stop for those traveling in the indicated direction: it does not permit entry in that direction.
A steady amber arrow warns of a stop in the indicated direction: stop if you can do so safely; otherwise clear the junction promptly and cautiously.
A flashing amber arrow does not always require a stop: it indicates that you should cross in the indicated direction with particular caution.
An upward green arrow permits travel straight ahead, not turning in any direction.
A red arrow requires a stop for the indicated direction: it does not order a right turn, even with caution.
Amber can flash while red and green are off: in that case proceed slowly and cautiously, observing priority rules.
Flashing amber calls for caution: proceed at moderate speed and observe priority rules.
A flashing amber light draws attention to a hazard; it does not give priority or require an unconditional stop. Slow down and proceed cautiously, observing priority rules.
Flashing amber does not always require stopping: proceed at moderate speed, cautiously and observing priority rules.

Flashing amber and red are not a combined danger signal in the normal operation of the same traffic light: red requires stopping, while flashing amber allows you to proceed cautiously and observe priority rules. Amber can flash with the other lights off.
Flashing amber requires moderate speed and caution, not clearing the junction quickly. With steady amber, anyone already in the junction must clear it promptly.
At steady amber, stop before the line if you can do so safely. If you are too close to stop safely when it appears, proceed and clear the junction promptly and cautiously.
A flashing amber arrow allows you to proceed in the indicated direction, slowing down and taking particular care.
If the signal is off, proceed at minimum speed and with particular caution, observing signs and priority rules; obey any working repeat signals.
Red requires stopping before the stop line even if no other vehicle is crossing the junction.
Red requires stopping, not proceeding: if it applies to all directions, you cannot enter the junction in any of them.
The red arrow requires you to stop for the direction shown, even if no other vehicles are approaching.
The two alternating red lights warn that the half barriers are closing and are placed at the level crossing.
The alternating red lights warn that the crossing is closing: when they operate, pedestrians must stop too.
The alternating lights give advance warning of closure for the train and remain on while it passes; wait until they stop.
The alternating red lights require you to stop, not to cross the railway quickly.
When the alternating red lights operate, crossing is forbidden: stop even if you could cross quickly.
The alternating red lights are provided for half barriers and some crossings without barriers; a steady red light is provided for full barriers.
A dashed line marks the lanes without being an uncrossable boundary, unlike a solid line: it may be crossed for a permitted maneuver if the other rules are followed.
A dashed line may be crossed to occupy the opposite lane temporarily while overtaking, if the maneuver is permitted and safe.
A dashed line does not prevent crossing it to make a U-turn, if the maneuver is safe and no other rule prohibits it.
Do not drive astride the line, even if it is dashed: you may cross it to change lanes.
A simple dashed white line does not identify a cycle track: a track without raised protection is separated from traffic lanes by a double solid white and yellow line.
On a single carriageway with two lanes in each direction, two solid lines separate opposing traffic; dashed lines can instead separate lanes.
A dashed center line separates lanes but, unlike a solid line, may be crossed for a permitted maneuver in compliance with the other rules.
A solid center line marks a boundary that must not be crossed; a dashed line may be crossed when the other rules permit it.
A solid line prohibits crossing it, not every overtaking maneuver: overtaking without crossing is possible if there is enough space and it is otherwise permitted.
Do not cross or drive astride a solid line: stay on your own side.
Lines separating opposing traffic are white; blue is not the color of the center line.
Do not cross a solid center line to turn left: use a place where the maneuver is permitted.
A series of studs used as a road marking indicates a solid line, not a dashed one. Retroreflective devices that reinforce a marking are a separate case.
The double solid line separates opposing traffic and is a boundary that must not be crossed.
The double solid line prohibits crossing it, but does not by itself prohibit overtaking entirely without crossing it when the other conditions permit.
A U-turn would require crossing the double solid line, which is prohibited; find a permitted place.
The double solid line separates opposing traffic with a boundary that must not be crossed, even to turn left. Turn where it is permitted.
The double solid line shown separates opposing directions of traffic; it does not mark lanes on a one-way road.
Both lines are solid: they must not be crossed, even when the other traffic rules are respected.
The arrows indicate the manoeuvres for each lane: choose the lane suited to your intended direction.

While the lane line is broken, you may change lanes subject to the other rules; you are not yet bound to stay in your current lane.
The figure does not show only straight arrows: it also shows a left arrow and a combined straight-and-right arrow for the respective lanes.
A solid line cannot be crossed to change lanes: select your lane earlier, while changing is still permitted.
Diagonal hatching marks traffic islands or advance warning areas excluded from traffic; they are not parking spaces.
White diagonal stripes mark a flush traffic island or the advance warning area for a raised island, directing vehicles around it.
Diagonal hatching marks an area closed to traffic, bounded by guide lines that channel vehicles.
Hatching for traffic islands consists of white diagonal stripes, not transverse blue lines.
Diagonal hatching marks islands or advance warning areas where parking is not allowed; parking bays have their own markings.
Diagonal hatching marks areas closed to traffic, not a lane to drive along merely at reduced speed.
Alternating yellow and black segments on the curb mark a stretch where parking is prohibited.
The alternating segments are painted on the vertical face of the curb and mark a no-parking stretch.
The yellow and black sequence on the curb marks the stretch of road subject to the parking prohibition.
Yellow and black segments on the curb indicate no parking, not a space reserved for public transport.
These curb segments indicate no parking along the road, not an obstacle at its edge.
The yellow and black segments indicate no parking; by themselves they do not indicate a no-stopping restriction.
The yellow outline with zigzag ends marks a scheduled bus stop area.
The zigzag sections are manoeuvring areas that let the bus pull in and rejoin traffic.
Parking is prohibited throughout the bus stop area, including the zigzag sections reserved for bus manoeuvres.
The markings prohibit parking in the stop area; a brief stop is possible if it does not obstruct traffic and no other prohibition applies.
The figure marks a scheduled bus stop area where parking is prohibited; it does not prohibit mopeds from passing.
Parking is prohibited within the marked area, including the zigzag ends. The 15 metres are measured from the bus stop sign when the spaces are not marked out.
The yellow zigzag marks a public transport stop: parking here is prohibited for mopeds too.
There are no arrows in the figure reserving lanes for turns, so all three lanes allow traffic to continue straight.
The left lane provides the position for a left turn; the figure has no arrows reserving it for turning, so it also permits going straight.
In the configuration shown, traffic in the middle lane continues straight; the outer lanes provide the positions for turning.
The right lane is not reserved for turning: without arrows, it also allows traffic to continue straight.
You cannot cross the solid line between lanes to change lanes; choose your lane earlier, where the line is broken.
In the configuration shown, the lanes do not all allow the same turns: the left lane allows a left turn, the right lane a right turn, and traffic in the middle lane continues straight.
The arrow in lane A indicates a left turn only; it does not allow you to go straight.
The combined arrow in lane B indicates both a left turn and going straight.
Only the arrow in lane C includes the right turn; the others do not.

Lane C is not just for turning: its combined arrow also permits going straight.
The broken center line may be crossed with the whole vehicle to overtake, provided the other conditions for the maneuver are met.
The broken line does not prohibit crossing it to make a U-turn; other prohibitions and safety requirements still apply.
The broken line may be crossed to turn left, respecting right of way and the other rules for the maneuver.
A broken line alone does not always make overtaking lawful: sufficient visibility and space are needed to complete it without danger or obstruction.
A broken line does not authorize overtaking on a bend merely because it is in town. Exceptions to the ban depend on the road layout and markings.
A broken line may also be crossed at a painted segment, subject to the other rules; you need not cross only at a gap.
The figure shows two marked lanes in each direction: in this configuration overtaking can be permitted on a bend, subject to the other conditions for the maneuver.

The double solid center line separates opposing traffic and cannot be crossed to make a U-turn.
Overtaking is normally done to the left of the vehicle ahead; overtaking on the right is allowed only in particular cases.

The parallel white stripes form a zebra crossing, marking where pedestrians cross the roadway.

The zebra stripes mark a pedestrian crossing, not an area closed to vehicle traffic.
The stripes mark a place for pedestrians to cross, not an area where they are forbidden to pass.
The zebra stripes mark a pedestrian crossing; a cycle crossing has a different boundary made of broken lines.

The line separates lanes on the same carriageway; it does not create two separate carriageways.

A U-turn would require crossing the solid line, which the marking prohibits.
The solid longitudinal line separates the lanes and must not be crossed.
The solid line prohibits crossing it, not every overtaking maneuver. Overtaking remains possible if it can be completed without crossing the line and while respecting the other rules.
The central line shown separates lanes on the carriageway; it does not identify a cycle path.
You cannot drive astride the solid line, which must not be crossed.
On a two-way road a U-turn across the solid line is prohibited because the line must not be crossed.
The cross and letters PL on the roadway supplement the vertical signs and warn that a railway level crossing is nearby.
The cross and PL mark a nearby level crossing: approach carefully and obey its signs.
In the section shown, the solid dividing line must not be crossed to move to the left side of the carriageway.
The cross and PL indicate a nearby level crossing, but do not specify a fixed distance of 150 meters.
The cross and PL indicate a nearby railway crossing without specifying whether it has barriers.
The cross and PL refer to a railway level crossing, where a road meets a railway, not an intersection of two roads.
The solid transverse line is the limit before which to stop when a stop signal requires it, for example a STOP sign.

With the STOP sign and marking, the solid line marks the limit before which to stop, even if no vehicles are approaching.
The line shows where to stop for a requirement, such as a red light or STOP sign; it does not require a stop at every uncontrolled junction.

The solid line is a stop line, used for example with STOP. A broken transverse line is used for GIVE WAY.

The two rows of squares mark a cycle crossing, intended for bicycles, not motorcycles or mopeds.

Speed must suit actual conditions to avoid danger to everyone, including people outside the vehicle.
An unsuitable speed can obstruct traffic: adapt it to conditions, also avoiding driving unnecessarily slowly.
You must keep control and be able to stop promptly within the visible distance and before foreseeable obstacles.
Rain or poor visibility changes driving conditions: speed must also suit the weather.
The length of the journey does not determine speed: road, traffic and vehicle conditions matter.
Safety concerns everyone, not just the passenger: speed must suit traffic conditions.
Being in a hurry does not justify an unsuitable speed: consider road, traffic and vehicle conditions.
Road characteristics and conditions affect driving: speed must allow you to retain control.
The condition of the vehicle, including brake efficiency, matters when choosing a speed that allows control and prompt stopping.
Adapt speed to traffic to avoid danger and obstruction.
The tire brand does not determine speed: the vehicle’s condition and the ability to control it matter.
Distance to the destination does not determine speed: adapt it to road and traffic conditions.
A schedule does not determine speed: adapt it to actual traffic conditions.
When passing an oncoming vehicle is difficult, slow down and stop if necessary to allow safe passage.
Glare reduces visibility: slow down and stop if necessary to retain control.
A hesitant pedestrian in your path may move unpredictably: slow down and stop if necessary.
An uphill stretch alone does not require slowing down and, if necessary, stopping; speed must still be adapted to actual road conditions.
Not every sign requires slowing down or stopping: obey its specific instruction and adapt speed to conditions.
Nighttime alone does not require slowing down and, if necessary, stopping; speed must still be regulated according to visibility and actual conditions.
Road features such as bends and visibility affect the speed at which you can maintain control.
Rain, fog and other weather conditions can change visibility and road conditions, so speed must be adapted to the situation.
Speed must allow you to stop within the visible stretch; adjust it when you cannot see as far.
The length of the trip does not determine your speed: adapt it to the actual road and traffic conditions.
The speed of vehicles behind does not by itself determine yours: choose a safe speed for the road, traffic and other conditions.
The type of fork alone is not the criterion for choosing speed: the vehicle’s characteristics and condition and the road conditions matter.
Adjust speed to the vehicle, road and traffic conditions to avoid danger and disruption to traffic.
An appropriate speed allows you to maintain control and safely make necessary maneuvers, including stopping for a foreseeable obstacle.
A slippery surface can make the vehicle harder to control and stop, so speed must be adjusted to the road conditions.
Hurrying or the time available does not determine the permitted speed: adapt it to safety conditions.
There is no general duty to always exceed 40 km/h: speed must suit conditions, which may require slowing down or stopping.
Speed is not proportional to the length of the route: adapt it to actual traffic conditions.
The road’s characteristics and condition are factors to consider in maintaining a speed that creates no danger.
Traffic is one of the conditions to consider: speed must allow travel without creating danger or disruption.
When visibility is limited, choose a speed that leaves enough visible distance to react and stop before a foreseeable obstacle.
The duty applies both by day and by night; particular attention to speed is required at night.
Speed must suit conditions even when no officers are present: the duty does not depend on enforcement.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the wording is ambiguous: speed must also be adjusted on one-way streets, as on any road, according to the conditions. A one-way street alone does not automatically require slowing down.
On bends, speed needs particular adjustment to maintain control and respond to conditions on that stretch.
Near junctions, speed needs particular adjustment so necessary maneuvers can be made safely.
Fog and mist reduce visibility: adjust speed so you can stop within the visible field.
Speed racing is prohibited; adjusting speed serves traffic safety, not competition with other vehicles.
Being outside a built-up area is not in itself a situation requiring particular adjustment: speed must still suit actual conditions, including outside built-up areas.
Daylight itself does not require particular adjustment: speed must always be adapted, including at night, when particular attention is required.
When visibility is limited, speed needs particular adjustment so you can stop within the visible stretch.
Near schools, speed needs particular adjustment, taking into account the possible presence of children.
Visibility may be reduced at night, so adjust speed to keep control and stop in time.
The following vehicle’s engine size is not the criterion for choosing speed; road and traffic conditions and other relevant circumstances matter.
A one-way street alone does not call for a special speed adjustment; speed must still suit actual conditions such as visibility and traffic.
Speed must suit the circumstances every day, not only on public holidays.
The gap to the vehicle ahead must allow you to stop in time if it slows or stops, avoiding a rear-end collision.
The vehicle travels during the reaction before braking; slower reactions require more distance to respond.
Speed affects the distance covered during reaction and braking, so it must be considered when leaving a gap ahead.
There is no fixed distance suitable for every situation: adjust it to speed and the condition of the vehicle and road, among other factors.
The requirement also applies while moving at 30 km/h or less: the gap must allow you to stop without a collision.
The obligation applies to vehicles following another vehicle, not only to pairs of mopeds.
At higher speeds more distance is covered during reaction and braking, so the necessary gap may increase.
The vehicle keeps moving during reaction time; a longer reaction means more distance covered before braking.
Less effective brakes can lengthen braking distance, so allow for their condition in the gap ahead.
Tyres in poor condition can increase stopping distance; adjust the gap to the vehicle’s condition too.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The gap to the vehicle ahead must allow you to stop in time, taking speed, reaction and conditions into account. The wording does not clarify possible indirect effects of road width.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The gap to the vehicle ahead must allow you to stop in time, taking speed, reaction and conditions into account. The wording does not clarify possible indirect effects of traffic behind.
The gap ahead must leave enough room to stop in time and avoid a collision if the vehicle ahead slows or stops.
The vehicle’s condition affects stopping: for example, less effective brakes may require more room.
Leave room to react and brake in time if the vehicle ahead slows or stops, avoiding a collision.
There is no general minimum gap of 150 metres: the required distance varies with conditions, subject to any specific requirements.
Speed matters: as it increases, reaction and braking distances increase, so a larger gap may be needed.
A gap from the vehicle ahead is required for moving vehicles generally, not only motorised quadricycles.
Overtaking requires enough clear space to complete the manoeuvre safely; if there is not enough, do not start.

The quiz marks this VERO. On a single-carriageway road with one lane in each direction, overtaking is prohibited near a hill crest. However, the question does not specify the number of carriageways: the Highway Code also provides an exception for roads with two separate carriageways and appropriate road markings.
Before overtaking, check that no driver following on the same carriageway or half-carriageway has already begun overtaking; if it is divided into lanes, check the lane immediately to your left.
A vehicle stopped to let pedestrians cross can hide them from view: overtaking it risks hitting them. Wait for them to cross safely.
A one-way street does not itself prohibit overtaking. You must still obey the applicable signs and markings and have adequate visibility and space.
A right indicator signalling a stop does not automatically prohibit overtaking: normally pass on the left, only if it is safe.
A moped may be overtaken when the manoeuvre is permitted and safe, leaving adequate lateral clearance.

On a bend on a two-way carriageway with one lane each way, the view may not allow you to check for oncoming traffic. The prohibition has exceptions, including for separate carriageways with the required road markings.
Without barriers or traffic lights, overtaking near a level crossing is prohibited: the area where a train may arrive must be kept clear.
Even if vehicles are stopped at a traffic light, you cannot cross a solid longitudinal line to pass them.
Separate carriageways do not create a general overtaking ban. Signs and safety conditions must still be respected.
A built-up area does not by itself prohibit overtaking: for example, it may be allowed on a straight stretch with sufficient visibility and space, subject to signs, markings and intersection rules.
Darkness does not automatically prohibit overtaking: sufficient visibility and space are needed to complete it safely.
If the vehicle ahead in the same lane has signalled an intention to overtake, wait: it could move into the space you intend to use.
Without a refuge, passengers board or alight on the carriageway: you cannot pass on the right of the tram stopped for them.

In poor visibility on a two-way carriageway with one lane each way, oncoming vehicles are difficult to check. The law provides exceptions, including for separate carriageways with the required road markings.
Rain alone does not prohibit overtaking, but do not overtake if visibility or conditions prevent a safe manoeuvre.
On a bend, overtaking may be permitted with at least two lanes in the same direction and suitable road markings; conditions must still be safe.
On a one-way carriageway, overtaking near a hill crest may be permitted; sufficient visibility and compliance with road signs and markings are still required.
The indicator warns others of your movement: signal before starting the manoeuvre.
When normally overtaking on the left, leave adequate lateral clearance to avoid contact while alongside.
There must be enough clear space to complete the entire manoeuvre, considering vehicles ahead and oncoming traffic.
There is no general ban on overtaking at night on a provincial road: adequate visibility and space are still required.
A motorcycle is also normally overtaken on the left; passing on the right is allowed only in particular cases.
You do not always have to sound the horn on a bend: use it moderately for safety; it does not make a prohibited overtake legal.
A solid longitudinal line cannot be crossed: if overtaking requires crossing it, the manoeuvre is not allowed.
Do not overtake when approaching a level crossing without barriers or traffic lights: you need to be able to check for an approaching train and stop before the tracks if necessary.
A vehicle stopped to yield may hide the traffic passing in front of it: overtaking it could cross that traffic’s path. Wait and respect the right of way.
On a one-way carriageway, a hill crest does not automatically prohibit overtaking: the required road signs and markings and other safety conditions must be in place.
A signal to pull over to the right does not by itself prohibit overtaking: pass on the left only if it is safe and permitted.
A moving tram on track that is not reserved is overtaken on the right when there is enough room; on a one-way carriageway, the left may also be used.
If the vehicle ahead accelerates while the overtaking vehicle keeps its speed, the speed difference decreases: overtaking takes more time and road.
A longer vehicle requires you to travel farther relative to it before you can safely return.
The difference in speeds determines how quickly you gain ground on the vehicle ahead and therefore affects the space needed.
Clear space is essential: it must be enough to complete the overtake safely, taking other road users into account.
Length matters: the longer the vehicle being overtaken, the more distance must be gained before returning.
On a one-way carriageway, a hill crest does not automatically prohibit overtaking: the required road signs and markings and safe conditions are needed.
With separate carriageways, a hill crest does not automatically prohibit overtaking: the required road signs and markings and safe conditions are needed.
On the downhill side of a hill crest, the view may become clear again and overtaking may be permitted. Sufficient visibility and space are still required, and no other prohibition must apply.
Not always: near a hill crest, visibility may be insufficient and overtaking is prohibited except for the specified exceptions concerning carriageways and road signs and markings.
Following another vehicle too closely reduces visibility and stopping margin. Before overtaking, keep a safe distance and ensure sufficient visibility.
Fog reduces visibility: do not overtake to avoid a rear-end collision; adjust speed and distance to the vehicle ahead.
The stopped vehicle may hide pedestrians who are crossing: overtaking it could endanger them. Wait for them to cross safely.
The following vehicle’s indicator warns that it may start overtaking: check your mirrors and wait to avoid interfering with its maneuver.
The no-overtaking sign prohibits overtakes covered by its restriction, even if the road appears clear.
A broken line may be crossed while respecting the other rules: by itself it does not prohibit overtaking.
An amber flashing light alone does not prohibit overtaking; the manoeuvre still requires space, visibility and safety.
On a one-way carriageway, a bend or hill crest does not automatically prohibit overtaking: the required road signs and markings and safe conditions are needed.
You may overtake on the right when the vehicle ahead has signaled and begun a left turn, provided there is enough space and the maneuver can be made safely.
A moving tram on track that is not reserved is overtaken on the right when the width of the carriageway allows it.
The type of vehicle and available space alone do not permit overtaking on the right: normally you overtake on the left.
A one-way road, including outside a town, does not by itself permit overtaking on the right: normally you pass on the left.
Slow traffic alone does not permit overtaking on the right; the specific exceptions in the road code apply.
Visibility must allow you to judge the space needed and complete the overtake without danger or obstruction.
A sign prohibiting overtaking must be obeyed even if the road looks clear.

The quiz marks this VERO, but does not specify where the other driver is. The statement appears to refer to checking the driver behind: before overtaking, check that they have not already begun overtaking on the same carriageway or half-carriageway, or in the lane immediately to your left where lanes are marked. Also check that the driver ahead in the same lane has not signaled the same maneuver.

The fact that an oncoming vehicle has ten meters in which to stop does not by itself show that overtaking is safe: there must be enough clear road to complete it, considering the difference in speeds and oncoming traffic.
The vehicle ahead slowing down does not itself prohibit overtaking; check that visibility and space are sufficient and the maneuver is safe.
An all-clear from the driver ahead is not required: the overtaking driver must personally check that the maneuver can be made without danger or obstruction.
The driver being overtaken must facilitate the maneuver without accelerating; on a road with one lane each way, they must keep as far right as possible.
The driver being overtaken must also avoid creating danger or obstruction, facilitate the overtake and not accelerate.
Drivers must not race: the driver being overtaken must facilitate the maneuver and not accelerate.
Not accelerating helps the overtaking driver complete the maneuver; the driver being overtaken is required not to accelerate.
The driver must not accelerate, but need not always slow down. In certain conditions a slow or bulky vehicle must slow down to let others pass.
Being overtaken does not require the right turn signal: facilitate the overtake and do not accelerate. The signal indicates a maneuver, not simply that someone is overtaking.
Do not move to the center to prevent other overtakes: facilitate the maneuver and, with one lane each way, keep as far right as possible.
Accelerating to create a slipstream hinders overtaking: the driver being overtaken must facilitate it and not accelerate.
To turn right, keep as close as possible to the right edge: this keeps your path near the edge instead of cutting unnecessarily across the roadway toward the right.
Signal the turn sufficiently in advance with the direction indicator so others know your intention.
As you approach the intersection, adjust speed to the conditions to maintain control during the turn.
To turn right, keep as close as possible to the right edge, not the left: this limits the space you occupy on the roadway and leaves room for traffic.
To turn right, do not move into the left lane: keep as close as possible to the right edge, limiting the space you occupy on the roadway and leaving room for traffic.
To turn right, do not move to the center of the intersection: keep as close as possible to the right edge, limiting the space you occupy on the roadway and leaving room for traffic.

On a two-way roadway, approach the center line as closely as possible to turn left. This prepares you for the turn while leaving space on your right for following vehicles where the road is wide enough.

Normally, turn near the center of the intersection, leaving it on your right, unless signs indicate otherwise. This path leaves room for an oncoming vehicle also turning left; you must still respect right-of-way rules.
When paths cross, yield to traffic from the right unless signs indicate otherwise; turning left does not remove this obligation.
On a two-way roadway approach the center line, not the left edge, which is the reference for a one-way roadway.
Speed does not replace yielding: use caution, respect the applicable right of way and turn without danger or obstruction.
You do not always yield to traffic from the left: normally you yield to the right, unless signs say otherwise. A turn also requires attention to oncoming vehicles.
Moving close to the right edge before turning lets you make the turn from the turning side without needlessly crossing the path of other vehicles.
On a two-way carriageway, move as close as possible to its centre line while remaining on your own half before turning left.
The indicator tells others about the manoeuvre: activate it in advance and keep it on until the manoeuvre is complete.
You do not always go around the centre: normally you turn near it, leaving it on your right, unless signs say otherwise.
The horn is not the ordinary turn signal: use it sparingly for safety; signal the manoeuvre with the direction indicators.
The turn must end in the part of the new road intended for your direction of travel: entering against traffic exposes you to a head-on conflict with vehicles travelling in the permitted direction.
At a junction, priority normally goes to traffic from the right unless signs say otherwise; also consider oncoming vehicles.
Normally turn near and to the left of the centre of the junction, leaving it on your right; signs may specify otherwise.
The right lane is not always the choice: to prepare for a left turn, approach the centre line, or the left edge on a one-way carriageway.
Looking only right is not enough: check traffic in other directions, including oncoming traffic, to turn without danger.
On a one-way carriageway, moving close to the left edge before turning lets you turn from the turning side without cutting across the path of vehicles on your left.
Even from a one-way road, normally turn near the centre of the junction, leaving it on your right, unless signs say otherwise.
A one-way road does not remove the normal priority to traffic from the right at a junction: it applies unless signs say otherwise.
You do not always yield to the left: at a junction priority normally goes to the right unless signs say otherwise.
A seemingly empty junction does not rule out the need to slow down: on approach, adjust your speed to the conditions and visibility.

Not just any lane will do: on a one-way carriageway, move close to the left edge to turn left, respecting signs and markings. In built-up areas, on carriageways with at least two lanes in each direction, you may choose the appropriate lane for your direction at the next junction unless signs indicate otherwise.
Checking the space behind in the target lane helps avoid cutting off an approaching vehicle during the move.
The vehicle ahead could move into the same lane: checking its signal helps avoid conflicting paths. This check is explicitly required when overtaking.
Anyone changing lanes must check that they can do so without danger or obstruction, considering the position and distance of vehicles in the target lane.
Even if the lane seems clear, signal the change in advance with the indicators and keep the signal on throughout the manoeuvre.
Signal a lane change with the indicators, not the horn, which is reserved for safety needs.

You should not look for solid lines: a broken line may be crossed while respecting the other rules. When a solid line is paired with a broken line, the pair may be crossed from the broken-line side; you must still check that the lane change is safe and signal it.
On a moped too, join the vehicles waiting in line: keeping your place makes the approach to the junction orderly and predictable, avoiding conflicts with vehicles that may move or turn.
Signalling a turn sufficiently early lets other road users know your intention before the manoeuvre begins.
Vehicle paths can cross at an intersection, so exercise maximum caution even when you have priority.
Giving way to the right is the general rule, but signs can establish a different priority.
To turn right, keep as close as possible to the right edge; turning does not require overtaking on the left.
A green light allows you to proceed, but does not remove the duty of caution: adjust your speed as you approach the intersection.
Broken lines do not authorize zigzagging: lane changes must be safe and signaled in advance.
A sudden change of direction leaves others no time to anticipate the maneuver: make sure it is safe and signal in advance.
U-turns are prohibited at and near intersections: the maneuver can interfere with vehicles approaching from other directions.

Low beams are not prohibited at intersections. For example, they are used while driving at night in a built-up area; outside built-up areas, high beams may replace them under the prescribed conditions.
Signal the turn in advance with the direction indicators and keep signaling throughout the maneuver.
There is no general 20 km/h limit for every intersection. Obey the applicable limits and adjust speed to the conditions.
Stopping is prohibited on pedestrian crossings and on sidewalks, unless signs allow it on the latter, to keep the passage clear.
A stop is a brief interruption of travel: it must not obstruct traffic, and the driver must remain ready to move off.
Both stopping and parking are prohibited on bends and hill crests; the prohibition protects traffic in places where visibility is critical.
The right edge is not always prohibited: subject to signs and other applicable rules, it is the side where a stopping vehicle should be placed.
Parking is prohibited in front of municipal waste bins, but a brief stop is not always prohibited. A brief stop must not obstruct traffic or violate other prohibitions.
The specific double-parking prohibition applies to parking, with an exception for two-wheeled vehicles. A brief stop must not obstruct traffic.
Stopping and parking are prohibited on and near level crossings to keep the railway crossing clear.
