Stopping is prohibited at and near intersections. In built-up areas the prohibition nearby applies at less than five meters from the extension of the nearest edge of the intersecting roadway, unless signs indicate otherwise.
Stopping on tram tracks is prohibited: the route must remain clear for rail vehicles.
Being near a sign alone does not prohibit stopping: it is prohibited if the vehicle hides the sign or another prohibition applies.
A road not divided into lanes does not itself prohibit a brief stop: where no other prohibition applies, you may stop near the right edge without obstructing traffic.
A no-stopping sign also prohibits a brief voluntary stop. A no-parking sign, by itself, does not prohibit a brief stop.
Stopping at the entrance or exit of a cycle track can block cyclists and hide them from other road users: access points must be kept clear.
A vehicle may not stop on a pedestrian crossing: the space must remain clear for pedestrians.
A long straight road does not itself prohibit a brief stop: where no other prohibition applies, you may stop near the right edge without obstructing traffic.
Normally, stop close to the right edge, parallel to it and facing the direction of travel, unless signs or another exception say otherwise.
The ban at a bus stop applies to parking. A very brief stop is possible only if it does not obstruct traffic and complies with any other applicable bans.
Normally, place the vehicle as close as possible to the right edge, parallel to it and facing the direction of travel, subject to exceptions.
The crossing must remain clear: both stopping and parking on a pedestrian crossing are prohibited.
A stop is a very brief interruption during which the driver remains ready to move off and must not obstruct traffic.
There is no general five-minute limit: a stop must serve a very brief need and the driver must remain ready to move off.
Both stopping and parking are prohibited on bends; the ban also applies near them outside built-up areas and on urban through roads.
Both stopping and parking are prohibited on hill crests; the prohibition also extends to their vicinity outside built-up areas and on urban through roads.
The level crossing and its approaches must remain clear: a stopped vehicle can obstruct traffic and leave other vehicles trapped on the tracks. Both stopping and parking are prohibited here.
Spaces reserved for taxis must remain available for the service: other vehicles may not park there.
Parking in front of municipal waste containers is prohibited so that the containers remain accessible.
Stopping and parking in a tunnel are prohibited unless signs say otherwise: the ban does not depend solely on lighting.
The general ban concerns the crossing itself, not every point nearby. Other bans or signs may nevertheless prohibit parking near the crossing.
Marked parking bays are intended for parking; any reservations, conditions and signs must still be respected.
Parking is prohibited at ramps and connections used by people with disabilities, which must remain clear.
Stopping and parking on tram tracks are prohibited, as is stopping or parking close enough to obstruct trams.
Reserved lanes are meant for public transport to travel in: a parked vehicle would obstruct its passage. That is why parking there is prohibited.
The ban also applies without yellow lines: where the space is not marked, parking is prohibited less than 15 metres from the stop sign.
A dangerous downhill slope does not by itself create a general parking ban. Signs and other applicable bans must still be observed.
A one-way street does not by itself prohibit parking. On urban one-way streets parking on the left is also possible if the required space for traffic remains.
In tunnels and under overpasses, a stopped vehicle can obstruct passing traffic. Both stopping and parking are therefore prohibited unless signs say otherwise.
Alternating yellow and black segments on the vertical kerb indicate a stretch where parking is prohibited.
Spaces reserved for vehicles serving people with disabilities are closed to unauthorised vehicles; they are for those entitled to use them.
A gaming hall does not by itself create a parking ban: signs and other bans applicable to the place still apply.
Stopping and parking on the pavement are prohibited unless signs say otherwise, so the ban is not absolute.
The prohibition applies near level crossings even when they have barriers.
The entrance must be kept clear so vehicles can enter and leave.
The sidewalk is for pedestrians: parking is prohibited unless signs indicate otherwise.
The prohibition applies even when the intersection is controlled by traffic lights: keeping it clear allows vehicles coming from other directions to pass.
A long straight stretch does not by itself prohibit parking: signs and other parking rules still apply.

A one-way street does not itself prohibit parking. On urban one-way streets, parking on the left is also allowed provided enough space remains for at least one line of vehicles, and in any case at least three metres in width.
Outside built-up areas, parking is possible under the applicable conditions: normally the vehicle is placed off the carriageway.
These spaces are reserved for vehicles serving authorised persons with disabilities; they are not freely available parking spaces.
In marked spaces the vehicle must stay within its own bay, without encroaching on adjacent bays.
The prohibition keeps access to roadside fuel stations clear during operating hours.
The absence of a sidewalk does not automatically prohibit parking: leave enough space for pedestrians, at least one metre.
Absence of street lighting alone does not prohibit parking; vehicle lights may nevertheless be required under the applicable conditions.
A slope alone does not create a general prohibition. The driver must nevertheless take the precautions needed to prevent accidents.
The exception to the double-parking ban applies to two-wheeled vehicles, not quadricycles.
A double-parked vehicle takes up road space and can obstruct traffic or block a parked vehicle.
Two-wheeled vehicles are excluded from the specific double-parking ban, but other rules still apply, including the duty not to cause obstruction.
Quadricycles do not qualify for the exception for two-wheeled vehicles: double parking is prohibited for them.
The specific double-parking ban excludes two-wheeled vehicles, including in built-up areas; other prohibitions and the duty not to obstruct still apply.
The double-parking ban for quadricycles has no exception for a few minutes. Parking is distinct from a very brief stop.
When joining the traffic flow, give way to vehicles already moving and manoeuvre without danger or obstruction.
Even in a car park, a vehicle must not block passage or prevent others from using their vehicles.
Where bays are marked, place the vehicle within its assigned space without encroaching on others.
Blue lines normally indicate paid parking; yellow lines mark spaces reserved for particular categories.
Blue lines normally indicate paid parking, not a space exclusively reserved for taxis.
Being close to an authorised car park does not itself create a general parking ban; signs and other parking rules still apply.
A driver joining traffic must yield to vehicles already moving normally and must not create danger or obstruction.
Before joining traffic, signal the maneuver well in advance so other road users can anticipate it.
The signal must begin well before joining traffic, not afterward, and continue until the maneuver is complete.
Turn off the indicator when the maneuver is complete, not upon reaching a particular speed.
Join traffic without danger or obstruction and at an appropriate speed; accelerating until the tires skid is not a safe maneuver.
The white stripes mark the part of the carriageway where pedestrians cross; they do not make the road an area closed to vehicles.

Without signals or an officer directing traffic, drivers must yield to pedestrians on or immediately near the crossing. Even when turning on green, yield to pedestrians on or immediately near a crossing at the entrance to the road being entered, when their passage is not prohibited.
The crossing is the marked part of the carriageway intended for pedestrians passing from one side to the other; it is not an area closed to vehicles.

Vehicles may pass over the crossing but may not park on it. Without signals or an officer directing traffic, drivers must yield to pedestrians on or immediately near it. Even when turning on green, yield to pedestrians on or immediately near a crossing at the entrance to the road being entered, when their passage is not prohibited.
The crossing is marked by white stripes on the carriageway, not blue ones.
The crossing is on the carriageway, so it is part of the road, and allows pedestrians to cross from one side to the other.
In a restricted traffic zone (ZTL), access and circulation are subject to the established restrictions: certain categories or authorized vehicles may be admitted.
A ZTL’s restrictions can apply at set times; follow the hours and conditions indicated for that zone.
Signs marking the beginning and end of a ZTL identify the area where its restrictions apply.
A ZTL is not automatically reserved for mopeds and bicycles: the permitted categories depend on the restrictions in force.
A ZTL restricts traffic by time or category: it does not always exclude every motor vehicle, since some may be permitted.
A ZTL restricts vehicle access and circulation under the zone’s rules; it is not defined as a restriction on pedestrian access.
A pedestrian area is normally closed to vehicles, with exceptions including bicycles and emergency vehicles; further signed restrictions or other permitted exceptions may apply.
Vehicles serving people with limited or impaired mobility are among the exceptions to the pedestrian-area ban, subject to the applicable conditions.

During an urgent service, police vehicles using both siren and flashing blue light may disregard traffic prohibitions, but must obey traffic officers’ signals and observe the rules of ordinary care and diligence.
Mopeds are not automatically allowed in pedestrian areas: vehicles are normally prohibited there, subject to the specified exceptions.
Merely keeping to 50 km/h does not authorize a quadricycle to enter: vehicles are prohibited in a pedestrian area, subject to the specified exceptions.
Being unpowered is not enough: cycles are among the exceptions to the pedestrian-area ban, but not all unpowered vehicles are automatically excepted.
The sidewalk is a part of the road outside the carriageway, intended for pedestrians.
Parking on the sidewalk is generally prohibited, but different signs or markings may permit it, for example in specially marked spaces.
The sidewalk is separate from the carriageway and intended for pedestrians: mopeds do not travel on it.
The sidewalk is intended for pedestrians and is separate from the carriageway used by moving vehicles.
The sidewalk is intended for pedestrians; the part reserved for bicycles is the cycle path.
The sidewalk is intended for pedestrians, not for parking vehicles; any exceptions must be signposted.
A pedestrian refuge provides a protected place where pedestrians can stop while crossing.
At a stop, a pedestrian refuge protects pedestrians and provides a place to board or leave public transport.
Steady yellow illuminated bollards marking a pedestrian refuge may be supplemented by flashing yellow traffic lights.
Steady yellow illuminated bollards mark a pedestrian refuge, making the protected island visible to drivers.
A pedestrian refuge protects pedestrians at crossings or stops; it is not intended for parking mopeds.
A pedestrian refuge is a protected space for pedestrians: mopeds travel on the carriageway, not over the refuge.
A pedestrian refuge is a protected space for pedestrians at crossings or stops, not a first-aid station.
Before changing direction, signal the maneuver well in advance to warn other road users.
Racing for speed is prohibited: as speed increases, so does the distance needed to stop before an obstacle.
An unnecessarily low speed can obstruct or endanger normal traffic; you must still slow down when conditions require it.
You may enter from a side road if you respect priority and make sure the maneuver is safe.
Speed must instead be adjusted to the road’s characteristics and condition to maintain control.

A brief stop at the right edge is not always prohibited: where stopping is allowed, place the vehicle as close as possible to that edge without causing danger or obstruction. Outside built-up areas, it must be placed off the carriageway; only if that is impossible should the right edge be used.
Ice reduces tire grip, making braking and maintaining control more difficult.
Leaves, especially when wet, can make the surface slippery and increase the risk of losing grip.
Loose gravel reduces grip and can cause loss of control, especially when cornering or braking.
Oil on the asphalt makes the surface slippery and can reduce grip, increasing the risk of losing control.
Pavement with adequate texture helps provide grip, including in wet conditions; it is not in itself a frequent cause of crashes.
Good lighting improves visibility of obstacles and helps prevent collisions with them, rather than being a frequent cause of crashes.
When approaching a tunnel, it is prudent to slow down before entering: the change in light can make obstacles harder to see.
At a tunnel exit, a crosswind gust can move the moped: holding the handlebars firmly helps control it.
The eyes need time to adjust from daylight to dim light. Slowing before entering helps you proceed as visibility changes.
Slowing gradually before a tunnel reduces the distance traveled while your eyes adapt to the light and avoids sudden braking that can endanger following traffic.
Sunglasses reduce the available light. Remove them before entering a tunnel to see better.
On wet roads grip decreases and stopping takes more distance. Reducing speed helps maintain control.
Stopping takes more distance on wet roads. A larger gap behind the vehicle ahead leaves more room to stop.
Grip is reduced on wet roads. Steering gradually helps avoid losing control.
Crossing a puddle fast is risky: water can hide its depth and reduce grip. Slow down and avoid it where possible.
Hard braking on a wet road can cause a loss of grip. Normally slow down and brake progressively; an emergency may require firm braking.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not explain what using the indicators “with caution” means. In rain, the specified maneuvers must still be signaled in advance; on wet roads, handle the handlebars carefully.
Drops on the visor can obstruct your view, making hazards and other vehicles harder to see.
A puddle can hide a pothole, making it hard to spot. In rain, slow down and ride smoothly.
Spray from vehicles ahead can obstruct your view. Leaving a larger gap helps you see and anticipate the road ahead.
Rain generally reduces grip rather than increasing it, so wheels can slip more easily on a wet road.
Rain does not in itself increase tire pressure. The main hazard is reduced grip on wet roads; check tire pressure when cold.
On wet roads grip decreases and braking distance tends to increase, not decrease.
With limited grip, sudden braking can cause a skid. Normally brake progressively; an emergency may require firm braking.
Wet roads offer less grip in a bend. Slowing before the bend and steering gradually helps maintain control.
Rain reduces grip and increases stopping distance. A larger gap behind the vehicle ahead leaves more room to stop.
The posted limit does not guarantee a safe speed in every condition. In heavy rain slow down because grip and visibility worsen.
Keeping the brake applied continuously downhill can reduce its effectiveness. Control speed using engine braking as well, if available, and the brakes when needed.
Wheels have less grip on wet roads. On a two-wheeled moped a skid can upset your balance and cause a fall.
Water reduces grip between tires and road, which can become slippery. Adjust speed and maneuvers accordingly.
Wet painted road markings can offer little grip, especially for two-wheelers. Approach them cautiously.
Water tends to reduce grip, not increase it. Wheels can slip more easily on wet roads.
With less grip on wet roads, braking distance tends to increase, not decrease.
On a wet road the tires have less grip than on a dry one, so the distance needed to stop increases.
When water cannot drain away fast enough, a film forms between tire and road, causing the wheel to lose contact and grip.
A badly worn tread drains less water, so under the same conditions aquaplaning can start at a lower speed.
Tread grooves let water escape from the contact area. If drainage is insufficient, the tire can lift onto a film of water.
The risk increases with speed, not with a reduction in speed: water has less time to escape from the contact area.
Aquaplaning removes grip and can cause skidding and loss of control instead of reducing them.
Tread depth matters: a badly worn tread drains less water, increasing the risk of aquaplaning.
Snow and ice reduce grip. A moderate speed gives the rider more chance to control the vehicle and stop.
Stopping distance increases on snow or ice, so a larger gap gives more room to stop.
With little grip, sudden acceleration can make the wheels slip. Accelerate gradually.
Braking hard on snow or ice can cause a skid. Slow down in good time and brake gently.
Accelerating fully when moving off can make the wheels slip on a slippery surface; accelerate gently.
Sudden steering on snow or ice can cause loss of grip and control. Anticipate the obstacle and maneuver smoothly.
Grip is more easily lost on a slippery bend: slow down before the bend and take it carefully.
With less grip, more distance is needed to stop. A larger gap helps you stop if the vehicle ahead slows down.
A moderate, as steady as possible speed reduces the need for sudden maneuvers, which can cause skids on a slippery surface.
Sudden acceleration can make the wheels slip. Travel slowly and accelerate gradually on a slippery surface.
Braking sharply in a bend can cause loss of grip. Slow down before the bend, braking progressively.
Sudden handlebar movements can cause loss of grip. On a slippery surface, maneuvers must be smooth and gradual.
Water on the road reduces grip between tire and asphalt, making braking and control more difficult.
Leaves, especially when wet, form a slippery layer between tire and road and can reduce grip.
Snow and ice make the road slippery: wheels have less grip and can slip more easily.
Oil forms a slippery layer on the asphalt and reduces tire grip on the road.
Low speed does not itself make the road less grippy. On a wet road, higher speed increases the risk of aquaplaning.
Engine speed alone does not determine grip between wheel and asphalt: road and tire conditions matter. Sudden acceleration can nevertheless make the wheel slip.
Road surface texture can improve friction between the tire and road; roughness alone does not reduce grip.
Longitudinal markings, when visible, help you follow the road and keep your position in reduced visibility.
Fog shortens the visible stretch of road: slow down so you can stop within that distance.
If it is no longer safe to continue, stopping off the carriageway reduces the risk of being hit by approaching traffic in poor visibility.
A vehicle stopped on the carriageway may be seen too late in fog. If you need to stop, look for a place off the carriageway.
Entering fog at speed leaves less time to react to what appears. Adjust your speed to the visibility instead.
Zigzagging creates unpredictable movements and risks for others. Keep control and follow a steady path.
The left indicator signals a maneuver to the left: leaving it on without that intention gives a misleading signal.
Do not sound the horn continuously because of fog: use it moderately, with the shortest possible signal, for safety.
Crosswinds can push the vehicle off course; moderating speed helps you keep control.
A gust can push the vehicle sideways: leaving clearance from obstacles at the side reduces the risk of hitting them.
On viaducts a vehicle can be exposed to sudden crosswinds that make it swerve, so take particular care.
Crosswinds do not require deflating the tires: pressure that is too low can impair handling. Maintain the pressure specified by the manufacturer.
Wind does not remove the need for a safe following distance: leave enough room to stop without hitting the vehicle ahead.
On leaving a tunnel, a crosswind can strike the vehicle suddenly. Moderate your speed rather than accelerating.
Following the direction allowed by the lane avoids a sudden maneuver at the junction; you can correct your route later.
A sudden lane change can obstruct or endanger others. Follow the selected lane and correct your route later.
Stopping near the junction to ask directions can obstruct traffic. Follow the lane and find a suitable place to stop.
Giving way does not authorize a turn different from the one assigned to the lane. Follow the permitted direction and correct your route later.
Pulling over and stopping near the junction can obstruct traffic. Follow the direction of the chosen lane instead.
Reversing toward following traffic is dangerous. Follow the chosen lane and correct your route later.
Pedestrians must be protected outside crossings too: slow down and stop if necessary to avoid hitting them.
In immediate danger a short horn blast can warn the pedestrian; also slow down and stop if necessary.
A pedestrian in your path may make it necessary to stop: reducing speed lets you stop promptly if needed.
High beams can dazzle the pedestrian and do not replace caution. If there is a risk of dazzling them, use dipped headlights and slow down.
Do not use the horn or other means to demand that the pedestrian move aside: allow them to complete the crossing.
Even outside a crossing, if the pedestrian has already started crossing, let them reach the other side rather than proceeding regardless.
Dipped headlights avoid dazzling the oncoming driver in return. Proceed cautiously and adjust your speed to visibility.
Do not stare at the headlights: look at the road ahead, avoiding the beam, to maintain your path without being dazzled.
Glare reduces what you can see: slow down and, if necessary, stop while maintaining control.
Using high beams in return can dazzle the other driver too. Use dipped headlights when passing and slow down if necessary.
Oncoming high beams do not automatically require hard braking, which could cause loss of control. Slow down and stop if necessary, keeping control.
Covering your eyes with your hands prevents you from properly controlling the road and vehicle. Avoid staring at the headlights, slow down and stop if necessary.
In heavy traffic, follow your lane’s flow only at a speed that allows you to retain control and a safe distance.
Even in a queue, leave enough space to stop without hitting the vehicle ahead if it brakes suddenly.
The horn is for safety, not for urging the vehicle ahead to speed up in slow traffic.
Do not constantly chase the clearest lane: each lane change requires checking and signalling and must not cause danger or obstruction.
Heavy traffic does not authorise a driver to use a lane reserved for public service vehicles if their vehicle is not permitted in it.
Zigzagging quickly makes manoeuvres and reactions difficult in traffic. Adjust your speed and make lane changes safely and with a signal.
Working lights help you see and be seen; the horn lets you warn others of danger. Checking them helps detect faults before riding.
Worn tread reduces grip, especially on wet roads. Checking its depth regularly helps identify tyres that need replacing.
The steering must move correctly so you can direct the vehicle. A pre-ride check can reveal faults needing repair.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but battery maintenance depends on its type: some safety checklists include checking electrolyte. Follow the vehicle manual and do not open sealed batteries; also check brakes, tires and lights.

Internal cylinder wear is measured with instruments during engine servicing; it is not the rider’s usual pre-ride check. Checks of tyres, controls and lights are more direct ways to help prevent accidents.
The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not clarify the role of maintenance: exhaust noise and mountings are inspected, while brakes and tires directly affect stopping and grip.
Hard or sharp objects worn on the body can injure you in a fall; avoid carrying them in areas that could be struck.
Excessive load can affect a moped’s stability and handling. Respect the vehicle’s limits and secure the load safely.
An upright but relaxed posture, without stiffening your back, helps reduce fatigue and maintain control of the moped.
Potholes and ditches can cause you to lose control of the moped; they are harder to see at night, so watch the road and adjust your speed to visibility.
A ringing phone does not justify sudden braking: stay in control and, if you need to stop, choose a permitted place and stop safely.
Rain alone does not require you to stop. Adapt your speed and increase your following distance on wet roads; if a dangerous situation requires it, you must stop.
With the same conditions and braking ability, braking distance grows with the square of speed: doubling speed makes it four times as long. This excludes reaction distance.
Brake pads and discs wear. Periodic checks can reveal wear or damage that impairs braking.
Drum brake shoes and drums can also wear or be damaged. Periodic checks help keep the brakes effective.
Prolonged braking can overheat the brakes and reduce their effectiveness. Avoid keeping them continuously applied.
On a slippery surface sudden braking can lock the wheels and cause a skid. Slow down and apply the brakes gradually.
You do not have to avoid all braking on uneven ground: slow down before the obstacle and use the controls carefully.
In hydraulic brakes, pressure transmits the control input when the brake is applied; it is not a value to keep low while riding. Check fluid level, leaks and braking effectiveness instead.
Underinflation can overheat and damage a tyre, risking loss of control. Check the pressure periodically when the tyres are cold and adjust it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
A badly worn tread provides less grip, especially in the wet, and can reduce braking effectiveness. Replace the tyre.
Pronounced wear on the shoulders can indicate low pressure, although it can have other causes. Check the pressure when cold.
Inflating above the specified pressure is not a reliable way to improve grip. Use the manufacturer’s recommended pressure.
Pressure that is too low can worsen handling and stability. Maintain the manufacturer’s recommended pressure rather than deflating to improve grip.
Insufficient pressure increases tyre flexing and heat, rather than improving cooling. Maintain the specified pressure.
Distraction, failure to give way and excessive speed are among the most frequent circumstances recorded in injury crashes: care and compliance with rules matter.
Among the most frequent circumstances in injury crashes are driver behaviours such as distraction and excessive speed.

Incorrect behaviour, such as failing to observe the road properly, often contributes to crashes. For example, among fatal collisions in Great Britain in 2022 with factors recorded, driver or rider error or reaction was the most frequent category; several factors can contribute to the same crash.
Vehicle defects can contribute to a crash, but driving errors such as distraction and failure to give way are among the most frequently recorded circumstances.
Bad luck does not identify a verifiable cause. Crashes are examined for concrete circumstances, including distraction, speed and failure to give way.

Road design can contribute to a crash, but it alone does not explain the most frequent causes. For example, among fatal collisions in Great Britain in 2022 with factors recorded, driver or rider errors or reactions were recorded more often than road environment factors; several factors can contribute.
An inexperienced driver may recognise a hazard later or make mistakes handling it, increasing crash risk.
An impaired state, for example due to alcohol or drugs, can impair driving and contribute to a crash.
Entering a bend too fast leaves less margin to maintain control and can cause a skid. Reduce speed before the bend.
Bad luck is not a technical cause of a crash: identify concrete circumstances such as a driving error or a road hazard.
The brand alone does not cause a crash. Concrete factors such as the rider’s behaviour and the vehicle’s condition matter.
A full-face helmet protects the head; wearing one is not in itself a cause of a crash. Still check traffic, including by turning your head.
Strong emotional upset can take your mind off riding and make it harder to pay attention to the road.
An animated conversation demands mental attention that is taken away from observing the road.
Alcohol impairs attention and judgment, making hazards harder to recognize and handle.
Coffee contains caffeine, a stimulant that can temporarily increase alertness; it does not replace rest.
Heavy traffic demands more attention; it does not in itself mean the rider’s attention decreases. Fatigue, however, can reduce it.
Cold does not necessarily reduce attention: its effects depend on exposure. Intense or prolonged cold can nevertheless impair it.
Worn tread drains water less effectively and can reduce grip on wet roads, increasing braking distance.
At higher speed more energy must be dissipated and, other conditions being equal, the vehicle travels farther while braking.
Grip is reduced on a wet road, so under otherwise equal conditions more distance is needed to stop under braking.
Tire condition matters: worn tread can reduce wet grip and lengthen braking distance.
Steering uses some available grip to change direction. Braking at the same time does not automatically shorten braking distance and can cause a skid.
A passenger adds weight and changes the vehicle’s handling; this does not guarantee shorter braking, and more stopping space should be allowed.

At 45 km/h you travel 12.5 m per second. For example, with an expected hazard, a 0.7-second reaction and effective braking on a dry surface, you travel about 9 m while reacting and 11 m while braking: about 20 m in total. This is a favorable estimate: reaction time, vehicle and road surface change the result.
At 45 km/h you travel 12.5 m in one second, or about 13 m rounded.
For a two-wheel moped, 45 km/h is the maximum design speed limit, not a speed that is always safe or mandatory.
At 45 km/h you travel 12.5 m in one second, about 13 m, not one meter.

The quiz uses an estimate of about 20 m, not 30 m. At 45 km/h, for example, with an expected hazard, a 0.7-second reaction and effective braking on a dry surface, you travel about 9 m while reacting and 11 m while braking. The distance is not fixed: in worse conditions, 30 m or more may be needed.
Assuming a one-second reaction time, at 45 km/h you travel 12.5 m before braking; braking distance is added to that. Less than 3 m is not a realistic stopping estimate.
Distraction can delay hazard recognition and reaction, during which the vehicle travels farther before braking begins.
The vehicle travels during the reaction time before braking; the longer this interval, the greater the total stopping distance.
At higher speed the vehicle travels farther during reaction, and braking distance also increases, other conditions being equal.
Stopping distance depends on distance traveled during reaction and braking, not the type of helmet. The helmet protects the head.
Reaction time matters: before the brakes are applied, the vehicle keeps moving, adding distance to the braking distance.
More worn tread does not necessarily shorten stopping distance: on wet roads it can reduce grip and lengthen braking distance.
A moped stopped in the middle of the road occupies traffic space: others may have to avoid it suddenly.
Riding side by side takes up more space and can obstruct other vehicles or make manoeuvring difficult.
Zigzagging involves unpredictable changes of path and can obstruct or surprise other drivers.
Parking off the road in a permitted place without blocking access or other users does not in itself obstruct road traffic.
A correctly executed right turn, after checking and signalling, does not in itself create danger or obstruction.
Stopping near the right edge, where permitted and without causing an obstruction, is not in itself dangerous. Local restrictions still apply.
When crossing tram tracks, give way to trams from either direction unless signs indicate otherwise.
When entering traffic, make sure the manoeuvre can be performed without danger or obstruction and let vehicles already travelling from either direction pass.
To make a U-turn, let traffic from either direction that conflicts with the manoeuvre pass and wait for a safe gap.
A flashing yellow light requires caution and moderate speed, but does not always require giving way to both sides: signs and normal priority rules apply.
When turning left, give way to oncoming vehicles; signs and other intersection rules still apply. You do not automatically give way to both sides.
A one-way street indicates the direction of travel on the crossing road, but does not by itself require giving way to both sides. Signs and intersection rules determine priority.
When leaving a parking place and entering traffic, let vehicles already travelling pass and check both directions.
When leaving a driveway and joining traffic, give way to vehicles already travelling on the road from either direction. If leaving a place not open to public passage, you must also stop.
A STOP sign requires you to stop at the stop line and give way to traffic on the road being crossed from either direction.
The priority-road sign indicates that drivers from other roads must give way at intersections. It does not require you to give way to both sides.
A pedestrian avenue does not create a general rule to give way to both sides; vehicle traffic in a pedestrian area is subject to the applicable restrictions.
At night there is no general duty to give way to both sides: signs and the rules applicable to the intersection still apply.
Third-party liability insurance protects both owner and driver against liability to others arising from circulation, within the coverage limits and conditions.
Third-party liability insurance covers compensable harm caused to others by the moped up to the policy limits; the excess is not covered by that limit.
Third-party liability insurance concerns compensation for harm to others arising from civil liability for circulation, including on mopeds; it does not cover every risk.
Third-party liability insurance compensates injury and property damage to third parties up to the coverage limits; not all damage to the driver or their vehicle is included.
Theft and fire affecting your own vehicle are not included in basic third-party liability insurance; separate optional coverage may be purchased.

Third-party liability insurance covers civil liability to others arising from circulation, not every form of liability. The premium is the price of coverage, not a proportional measure of all liabilities.
The policy limit is the maximum compensation payable by the insurer. If the damage exceeds it, the responsible party bears the excess.
Third-party liability insurance covers liability for damage to others, not damage to your own moped. The latter requires different coverage, if provided for in the contract.
The policy documents the contract: the insurer must issue it to the policyholder or provide another signed document.
The certificate proves insurance coverage. The rider must carry it with the registration certificate and show it on request.
The insurer issues the policy or another signed contract document; a complete accident prevention manual is not required.
The insurer issues the policy or another signed contract document, not an extract from the Civil Code.
The insurer issues the policy or another signed contract document, not a first-aid manual.

Riding without third-party liability coverage incurs an administrative penalty. For annual contracts or contracts lasting a year plus a fraction, after expiry the previous coverage continues until the new policy takes effect, for no more than 15 days.

If a vehicle is ridden without third-party liability coverage, it may be seized. For annual contracts or contracts lasting a year plus a fraction, after expiry the previous coverage continues until the new policy takes effect, for no more than 15 days.

A short journey does not permit riding without third-party liability coverage. For annual contracts or contracts lasting a year plus a fraction, after expiry the previous coverage continues until the new policy takes effect, for no more than 15 days.

An out-of-town road does not permit riding without third-party liability coverage. For annual contracts or contracts lasting a year plus a fraction, after expiry the previous coverage continues until the new policy takes effect, for no more than 15 days.

Being an adult does not permit riding without third-party liability coverage. For annual contracts or contracts lasting a year plus a fraction, after expiry the previous coverage continues until the new policy takes effect, for no more than 15 days.
The quiz marks this TRUE: a moving moped must be lit even in good weather. “Always” is imprecise, however: where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
The quiz marks this TRUE: the lighting requirement also applies by day. “Always” is imprecise, however: where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
The quiz marks this TRUE: the lighting requirement applies by day and night. “Always” is imprecise, however: where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
The quiz marks this TRUE: the lighting requirement also applies in built-up areas. “Always” is imprecise, however: where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
The requirement does not depend solely on street lighting: it also applies by day. Where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
Dipped headlights do not always replace main beams: the latter may be used outside built-up areas when external lighting is absent or insufficient, subject to the rules against dazzling others.
The lighting requirement also applies by day, not just at night. Where permitted, daytime running lights can replace dipped headlights if fitted.
A reflector returns light from another vehicle towards its source, so it can indicate the vehicle’s presence even with its lights off, if illuminated.
A reflector returns headlight light towards its source, so an illuminated detached trailer can be visible in the dark.
A reflector does not produce its own light: it reflects headlight light towards its source, making the vehicle’s presence visible.
When illuminated by another vehicle’s headlights, a reflector can make the vehicle visible even if its rear lights have failed. It does not repair or replace the required lights.
Reflectors reflect light. The rear reflectors specified for quadricycles are non-triangular; triangular ones identify trailers.
A reflector reflects light and signals the vehicle’s presence; it cannot indicate a turn or replace direction indicators.
Before moving out to overtake, signal your intention in advance with the direction indicator so others can understand the manoeuvre.
Signal a lane change sufficiently early and keep the indicator on throughout the maneuver.
Signal a turn, whether right or left, in advance using the corresponding indicator.
A stop required by a traffic light is not in itself a turn or lane change. A separate maneuver, such as a turn, must be signaled.
Simply traveling in your lane in parallel traffic does not require an indicator; signal when changing lanes.
Indicators are also needed for right turns and other maneuvers, such as changing lanes.
The quiz accepts a sideways arm signal before turning when the indicators have failed. They must be repaired as soon as possible: driving with required equipment that does not work is punishable.
Faulty indicators must be repaired: the vehicle’s devices must be kept in working order.

A lane change must be signaled in advance. The quiz teaching material advises a sideways arm signal if the indicators fail; they must be repaired, because driving with faulty required equipment is punishable.

The quiz does not treat the fault as an absolute ban on continuing. The teaching material says that an arm signal can be given before turning or changing lanes and the indicators repaired as soon as possible. Driving with required equipment that does not work is nevertheless punishable.

The quiz uses an arm extended sideways to signal a turn; when signal devices are absent, an arm raised vertically signals a stop. Faulty indicators must be repaired: riding with required devices that do not work is subject to a penalty.

The horn does not replace a turn signal: the quiz teaching material uses an arm extended sideways. Faulty indicators must be repaired: riding with required devices that do not work is subject to a penalty.
Before meeting an oncoming vehicle, switch to dipped headlights at a sufficient distance to avoid dazzling its driver.
When following a vehicle closely, use dipped headlights; a brief flash is allowed to signal an intention to overtake.
If high beams risk dazzling other road users, switch to dipped headlights.
Normally, steady high beams are not used in built-up areas; brief flashes for permitted warnings are allowed.

Half an hour before sunrise does not by itself impose a ban: outside built-up areas, high beams are permitted when external lighting is absent or inadequate. However, switch to dipped headlights before meeting a vehicle, when following one closely, and when there is a risk of dazzling; when following closely, a brief flash to signal overtaking is permitted.
The rule does not depend on the type of vehicle ahead: switch to dipped headlights when close behind, except for a brief flash to signal overtaking.
The normal ban on steady high beams in built-up areas does not depend on rain; permitted warning flashes remain allowed.
A brief flash can give a useful warning to prevent an accident, including during the day and in built-up areas.
A brief flash can warn the vehicle ahead of an intention to overtake; it does not automatically give the right to perform the maneuver.
Even during the day and in built-up areas, flashing can give a useful warning to prevent an accident or signal an intention to overtake.
Flashing to warn or signal overtaking is also allowed outside tunnels, by day and night.

Inadequate lighting is neither necessary for flashing nor sufficient on its own to justify it. Flashing is permitted to give useful warnings to prevent accidents or signal an intention to overtake the vehicle ahead, including during the day and in built-up areas.
During the day flashing is also allowed to signal an intention to overtake to the vehicle ahead, not only in immediate danger.
The horn is solely for road safety and must be used moderately and as briefly as possible.
In built-up areas the horn is prohibited except in real and immediate danger. The law also provides an exception when necessary for drivers transporting injured or seriously ill people.
Even when needed for safety, the signal must be brief and used moderately.
Outside built-up areas, the horn may be used when road or traffic conditions require it to prevent accidents.
Being near a hospital does not permit sounding the horn at all times: the conditions restricting its use still apply.
Overtaking does not always require the horn: outside built-up areas, use it when conditions require it to prevent accidents.
In built-up areas it is allowed in actual and immediate danger, including at night.
A crossing alone does not require sounding the horn: its use is subject to the conditions for preventing accidents.

A damaged sidewall can compromise tire safety. For motorcycle tires, Bridgestone says to replace tires with damage outside the tread because they cannot be properly repaired. Have a specialist examine the damage.
Sidewall damage can cause a sudden loss of pressure and make the vehicle difficult to control.
Sidewall damage can cause a tyre to fail suddenly: have the damage checked before riding.
Low speed does not eliminate the risk of a damaged tyre failing: have the damage checked and replace the tyre if it cannot be repaired.
You cannot assume that retreading will resolve sidewall damage: have the tyre examined. For example, Bridgestone calls for replacement when a puncture is outside the tread.
Sidewall damage can compromise safety and must not be ignored: have the tyre checked and replace it if the damage cannot be repaired.
With badly worn grooves, water drains less effectively and wet-road grip decreases, including when cornering.
An excessively worn tread is more vulnerable to penetration by objects on the road and therefore to punctures.
With badly worn grooves the tyre clears less water: reduced wet-road grip can lengthen braking distance.
Tread affects braking: when the grooves are badly worn, reduced wet-road grip can increase the distance needed.
Excessive wear does not improve wet-road grip: shallower grooves clear less water.
Even on dry roads an excessively worn tyre is more vulnerable to penetration by objects and punctures; its danger is not limited to rain.
For mopeds, the tread pattern, where required, must remain visible and the main grooves must retain at least 0.5 mm depth.
Checking the tread frequently helps detect wear and damage before the tyre becomes unfit for use on the road.
For mopeds the minimum depth of the main grooves is 0.5 mm; the pattern, where required, must be visible.
The prescribed minimum for the main grooves of mopeds is 0.5 mm, not 2.5 mm.
The minimum for the main grooves of mopeds is 0.5 mm; 1 mm is the minimum for motoveicoli, a category that includes motorcycles and motor tricycles.
Tread contributes to grip, especially on wet roads: excessively worn grooves clear less water.
Insufficient pressure increases tyre deformation and rolling resistance, so the engine consumes more fuel.
With insufficient pressure, the tread tends to wear sooner at the shoulders, or sides.
Insufficient pressure can make a tyre lose contact with the wet road and slide on a film of water.
An underinflated tyre flexes excessively and makes handling less precise, reducing stability.
Insufficient pressure tends to wear the tread shoulders most, not the centre.
Pressure that is too low does not improve performance: it can impair handling and increase wear.
Pressure can fall with use. Checking it regularly when the tyres are cold helps keep it at the prescribed value.
Use the pressure specified by the manufacturer for the vehicle and load; regular checks allow pressure loss to be corrected.
Checking the lights reveals faults that impair visibility and the vehicle’s signals.
Frequent checks can reveal faults before they impair the vehicle’s ability to stop.
Tyres should not be kept underinflated: inflate them to the pressure specified by the manufacturer.
Do not routinely inflate above the prescribed value: use the manufacturer’s pressure for the load conditions.
For a moped, the first periodic inspection is due in the fourth year, by the end of the month of first registration.
After the first inspection, periodic inspections are due every two years, by the end of the month corresponding to the last inspection.
A moped’s ordinary periodic inspection is not annual: after the first, it is repeated every two years.
Periodic inspections follow their own schedule: first in the fourth year and then every two years, not automatically at every new registration.
Brake pads and other braking components wear down; checking them allows replacement before they become too worn.
On hydraulic systems, check the fluid level: if it is low, check for wear and possible leaks.
Excessive lever travel can indicate a fault in the system; checking it helps identify the problem.
Checking the rims concerns wheel safety; it is not a specific check of the braking system. To keep the brakes effective, their condition, operation and controls are checked.
Routine maintenance does not require chemical analysis: check the fluid level and condition and replace it according to the manufacturer’s schedule.

Checking the tyre structure concerns the tyre; it is not a specific check of the braking system. Tyres remain important for grip; brake condition, operation and controls are checked to keep the brakes effective.
Using both brakes progressively applies braking to both wheels and helps maintain control.
Operating both controls progressively uses both the front and rear brakes while maintaining control.
Even on dry roads, brake progressively to avoid locking the wheels. In an emergency, react quickly and apply the brakes firmly without locking them.
Even on dry pavement, apply both brakes progressively: used together they can shorten stopping distance compared with one brake alone.
Do not use the front brake alone: even on dry pavement, apply both brakes to slow effectively.
Using just one brake is not the normal technique: applying front and rear progressively together can shorten stopping distance.
Using both brakes makes use of the braking capacity of both wheels; apply them in a controlled way.
Braking transfers load toward the front wheel. Moving your body weight rearward partly counteracts that transfer without eliminating it; use both brakes with control and avoid locking the wheels.
Brake firmly without locking the wheels: excessive pressure can make them skid and compromise control.
Do not use only the front brake: in an emergency, use both brakes and apply pressure in a controlled way.
The rear brake alone does not use the front brake’s stopping power: controlled use of both can shorten stopping distance.
Do not try to lock the wheels by braking in jerks: brake firmly and with control, avoiding wheel skid.

If the moped starts to skid under braking, easing braking effort gradually can help regain traction and control. Guidance differs for an already locked rear wheel; the question does not describe that case.
Braking instability can also be caused by uneven or defective brakes. Stop safely and have the vehicle checked; if it is unsafe, do not continue riding and arrange transport to a workshop.
Once stopped, check tyre pressure too: incorrect pressure can affect braking and stability.
Staying calm helps you avoid sudden manoeuvres and control the braking instead of reacting impulsively to the skid.

Engine oil level is a maintenance check, but it is not the priority check indicated by the quiz after a braking skid: once stopped, check the tires and brakes. A leak or other mechanical fault still needs attention.
Hard braking and sharp steering can exceed available grip and worsen a skid. Avoid abrupt maneuvers; guidance differs for an already locked rear wheel, which the question does not specify.
Abruptly releasing the throttle does not correct a braking skid: avoid sudden manoeuvres and control the braking. In an emergency stop, close the throttle smoothly.
Adjust the mirrors while stopped, after putting on your helmet, in the riding position and before setting off. A helmet can reduce your field of vision: check the rear view under riding conditions.
Adjust them while stopped, with the vehicle upright and the stand raised, in the riding position: the view then matches the one while riding.
Adjust mirrors before setting off so you can see traffic behind from the start without trying to adjust them while moving.
Adjusting mirrors from the riding position helps you see properly behind. The quiz sequence is to do this before setting off and after raising the stand; the order can depend on the stand type.
Do not wait until you have travelled some distance: adjust the mirrors before setting off so the rear view is available immediately.
Checking the controls before setting off lets you discover whether the brakes are not working properly before you need them in traffic.
An engaged anti-theft device can prevent movement or manoeuvring: disengage or remove it before setting off.
The steering must turn freely to manoeuvre: resolve any obstruction before setting off.
Adjusting the mirrors beforehand gives you a rear view from the start without having to set them while riding.
Checking the lights before setting off can reveal a fault affecting illumination and the visibility of the vehicle.
The spark plug is checked according to the model’s maintenance schedule; it is not a check to repeat before every trip.
Sunglasses are not always needed: dark lenses reduce visibility in low light.
The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not say why the throttle would be turned. Some manufacturer-specified checks instead verify that it moves and returns freely, including with the engine off.
Modifications that increase a moped’s speed beyond the prescribed limits are prohibited: the vehicle must retain its required characteristics.
A required silencer must be kept effective and must not be altered: tampering can reduce its ability to control noise.
A moped’s maximum design speed is 45 km/h; modifications capable of exceeding that limit are not permitted.
Riding with the front wheel raised is prohibited: without contact with the road, that wheel cannot steer or brake.
Dipped headlights are not prohibited in daylight: on mopeds they are normally required even in built-up areas, with the permitted alternatives for daytime running lights.
Switch off the engine when refuelling: fuel is flammable and possible ignition sources must be avoided.
The periodic inspection checks the vehicle’s condition, including its safety; it must be carried out when due.
Effective brakes allow you to slow down and stop; working lights help you see and be seen. Both must be kept working.
Periodic checks by a mechanic help identify faults and keep the moped in good condition; they do not replace the required inspection.
Mirrors help you observe traffic behind you: removing them reduces your view and does not improve safety.
Do not arbitrarily change the colours of the lights: keep the devices compliant so that light signals can be recognised.
Do not keep a moped’s lights off just because it is daytime: dipped headlights are normally required even in town, with the permitted alternatives for daytime running lights.
Riding alongside another moped to talk is not a safety check and can distract from riding: keep your attention and control of the vehicle.
While riding, a moped rider must wear an approved, fastened helmet; the rules provide specific exceptions for vehicles with particular protective equipment.
A helmet protects the head in impacts and reduces the risk of serious injury; it is compulsory while riding in the cases provided for.
The passenger too must wear and fasten an approved helmet while riding, subject to the specific exemptions provided for.
The rider’s helmet requirement does not end at 18: it also applies to adults.
Wear a helmet while riding in every season: the requirement is not limited to winter.
The requirement does not stop at 16: people over 16 must also wear a helmet on a moped.
The helmet requirement is not limited to tricycles: it also applies to riders of two-wheeled mopeds, subject to the specific exemptions provided for.
A correctly sized helmet fits the head well and, with the chin strap fastened, can provide better protection in an impact.
The helmet must fit snugly without moving freely: if it is too loose, it can come off in a fall.
For riding, a type-approved helmet is required: approval checks protective requirements, including impact absorption and retention system tests.
Not just any size will do: the helmet must fit snugly without being uncomfortable, or it may come off.
A helmet that is too loose can come off in a fall. Choose a snug, comfortable size.
The number of colors does not determine protection: choose an approved helmet that fits properly.
Scratches can cause glare and reduce visibility, so a scratched visor should be replaced.
The chin strap holds the helmet on your head: it must be intact and work properly so it can be fastened securely.
A cracked or scratched visor can impair visibility and should be replaced.
Do not keep using a scratched visor: scratches can cause glare, so replace it.
A completely fogged visor prevents you from seeing clearly: restore visibility before continuing.
Clean the visor carefully: dirt and insects can obstruct your view.
Replace the helmet after a crash involving a fall: the impact may have damaged internal parts that cannot be seen.
After a severe impact, replace the helmet even if it looks intact: damage may be invisible.
A scratch-free visor helps maintain a clear view; scratches can cause glare and mean it should be replaced.
The helmet must be type-approved: approval checks protective requirements, including impact absorption and retention system tests.
Do not alter the inside to make it wider: this may compromise protection. Choose a helmet of the right size.
Even without visible cracks, a severe impact can damage the inside of the helmet: replace it.
The chin strap must be properly fastened in summer too: if it is undone, the helmet can come off.
Adjust and fasten the chin strap securely so the helmet stays in place and does not come off.
The chin strap must be fastened snugly to hold the helmet, while still allowing you to open and close your mouth.
The helmet must fit snugly and the chin strap must be securely fastened, making it less likely to come off.
Properly fastening the helmet is compulsory while riding: an unsecured helmet can come off.
A loose chin strap can allow the helmet to come off. Fasten it snugly without preventing your mouth from opening.
Do not leave the chin strap loose: it must hold the helmet securely on your head.
Breaking the helmet requirement leads to administrative detention of the moped; the rule does not apply only to minors.
A lowered visor forms a barrier in front of the face; when raised, insects can strike the rider.
A helmet protects the head from impacts; without that protection a crash can cause serious injury.
A helmet is required on straight roads too: the shape of the road does not remove the obligation, subject to specific exemptions for protected vehicles.
Adults must also wear a helmet on a moped: adulthood is not an exemption. Specific exceptions apply to protected vehicles.
Without a helmet the head has less protection against impacts, and a crash can cause serious injury.

The quiz marks this VERO, but the wording is imprecise: from age 16 a minor may hold B1, which is also valid for AM vehicles. AM is therefore not the only possible licence for someone without A1, subject to any applicable restrictions.
Mopeds fall under category AM, for which the minimum driving age is 14.
The registration certificate records the moped’s identification and construction details, as well as its plate and registered holder; it must be carried.
The compulsory insurance certificate must be carried; it may also be presented digitally.
A1 is not essential: an AM licence already authorises riding mopeds.
The purchase receipt is not among the required road documents; the registration certificate is required instead.
The registration certificate identifies the moped and records its construction details, plate and registered holder; it must be shown to officers on request.
The compulsory insurance certificate must be available for officers to inspect, including in digital form.
The user and maintenance manual is not among the required road documents; the registration certificate must be presented instead.
The purchase deed is not a road document to present at a check; the registration certificate is required instead.
The tax code is not among the road documents required of the rider; an appropriate licence must be carried instead.
Category AM is available from age 14, the minimum age for driving its vehicles.

The quiz marks this VERO, but the wording is imprecise: from age 16 a minor may hold B1, which is also valid for AM vehicles. AM is therefore not the only possible licence for someone without A1, subject to any applicable restrictions.
An A1 licence also authorises driving AM vehicles, so a separate AM licence is unnecessary.
An appropriate licence is needed to ride a moped even without a passenger; AM is one category that authorises it.
A light quadricycle falls under category AM: a minor also needs an appropriate licence to drive one.
Renewal is not always every two years: the ordinary validity is ten years and decreases with age; from age 80 renewal is every two years.
The theory test checks knowledge, while the practical test checks driving skills and behaviour. Both must be passed to obtain AM.
Category AM includes three-wheeled mopeds and light quadricycles; it can be obtained from age 14.
When driving, carry a licence valid for the vehicle: if AM is the only licence held, carry it.
An AM licence permits riding a moped even without a passenger; carrying one also requires the conditions concerning age and the vehicle to be met.
An AM licence covers mopeds, not category A1 motorcycles; riding without a passenger does not broaden its scope.
Keeping to the right near the edge leaves room for traffic, including oncoming vehicles on a two-way road.
The opposing lane may be entered temporarily to overtake only when the maneuver is permitted and there is sufficient space and visibility; then return to the right.
In normal travel, use the rightmost free lane, even where there are three lanes in each direction.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but “both lanes” does not make clear whether it means using them in sequence or choosing either one. Normally you ride on the right; for a permitted overtake, ordinarily pass on the left and return right as soon as possible without danger, subject to the specified exceptions.

Three lanes in total for two directions do not by themselves allow travel in parallel lines: the ordinary rule requires at least two lanes per direction and dense traffic, subject to other prescribed cases.
An empty road does not remove the duty to keep right and stay near the right edge.
Moving as close as possible to the right edge when meeting another vehicle leaves more room for oncoming traffic.
On a bend on a two-way, single-carriageway road with one lane each way, visibility may be limited; keeping as far right as possible leaves room for oncoming traffic.
On a hill crest, on a two-way carriageway with one lane in each direction, visibility may be limited: keeping as far to the right as possible leaves room for oncoming traffic.

For example, on a bend on a two-way, single-carriageway road with one lane each way, keep as far right as possible. On a one-way carriageway, the general rule of riding near the right edge still applies.
To turn left, approach the center line of the carriageway or, on a one-way road, its left edge, after signaling and checking the maneuver.
To overtake, normally pass to the left of the vehicle being overtaken, leaving adequate lateral clearance, then return to the right.
Lanes reserved for public transport must remain clear: parking there is prohibited.
Parking on cycle tracks is prohibited because it would occupy space intended for cyclists.
The sidewalk is for pedestrians: parking is prohibited unless signs indicate otherwise.
Being near a sign does not always prohibit parking: the prohibition applies when the vehicle hides the sign from view, along with any other applicable restrictions.

In town, parking can be allowed without marked bays, for example along the right edge where no prohibition applies, provided the vehicle is positioned properly and signs and other restrictions are respected.
On urban one-way roads, parking on the left is also permitted if space remains for a line of vehicles and at least three meters in width.
The ordinary rule is to place the vehicle near the edge, parallel to it and facing the direction of travel; signs may provide otherwise.
A center stand, if fitted and used correctly, supports the moped while parked. Still check that it is stable on the ground.
The sidewalk is for pedestrians: parking is prohibited unless signs indicate otherwise.
During parking the engine must be switched off; parking is distinct from a very brief stop.
A short stay does not authorize occupying the sidewalk: the prohibition applies unless signs indicate otherwise.
Leaving room for pedestrians is not enough: parking on the sidewalk is prohibited unless signs allow it.
On a downhill road, the quiz says to park the moped on its center stand with the front wheel facing uphill. A slope can make the vehicle unstable, so always check that the stand supports it securely.
On a downhill road, park the moped with its front wheel facing uphill: facing downhill, it could roll and fall. Always check that it is stable on its stand.
A slope can make the moped unstable: check that the stand supports it firmly before leaving it.

Pointing the wheel toward the curb alone does not ensure stability: on a steep slope, if the vehicle faces downhill, it can make it unstable on its side stand. The quiz recommends facing the moped uphill.
The quiz directs you to face the front wheel uphill, not downhill. A slope can make the vehicle unstable, so always check that the center stand supports it securely.
There is no need to lean it against a wall: use a suitable stand and check that it is stable.
Unless signs say otherwise, priority to traffic from the right also applies to slow vehicles: their speed does not cancel the rule.
Taking account of other road users’ positions and movements lets you adapt your riding and avoid maneuvers that could cause collisions or force others to react abruptly.

Before signaling a lane change, check the mirror and blind spot: this helps you identify other vehicles and assess whether you can move safely. Signal in good time, check the blind spot again and move only if it is safe.

The quiz marks this VERO, but the statement is too absolute: during the day, outside the cases in article 153(1), daytime running lights, if fitted, may replace dipped headlights. Dipped headlights are required even by day in tunnels and in the poor-visibility conditions specified by law, subject to permitted substitutions.
Do not always ride in the middle of the road: normally ride on the right side of the carriageway, near its right edge.

Do not weave between queued vehicles: a driver may fail to see the moped and move suddenly, leaving little room to avoid a collision. Overtaking requires sufficient visibility and space and a maneuver that does not create danger.
Adjust speed to road and traffic conditions to retain control; do not travel fast merely to avoid holding others up.
On a broad bend, after adjusting speed, a little steady throttle helps keep the ride smooth and the suspension stable.
At the same speed a tight bend requires more lean: moderating speed helps you follow the curve while keeping control.
Abrupt inputs can upset your path: move the handlebars smoothly and progressively in a bend.
Slowing before entry lets you choose a suitable speed without having to brake sharply while the moped is leaned over.
Increasing speed at the beginning of a bend is not necessary for stability. Slow down before entering and take the bend at a controlled speed: excessive acceleration can make you run wide.
Moving toward the middle of the road to tighten the line does not guarantee stability and can expose you to oncoming traffic. Adjust speed before the bend and stay on your side of the carriageway.
Lifting the front wheel removes its contact with the road and the ability to steer normally; you can lose balance and fall.
On a two-wheeled moped, a wheelie is prohibited: lifting the front wheel removes the road contact needed for normal directional control.
With the front wheel raised you can lose control; a fall can cause the rider serious injuries.
A wheelie carries risks: the front wheel loses contact with the road, preventing normal steering and making a fall more likely.
On a two-wheeled moped, a wheelie is prohibited even when the road is clear: lifting the front wheel removes the road contact needed for normal directional control.
Riding with the front wheel raised is prohibited. Without front-wheel contact with the road, normal steering is lost, making the moped harder to control.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the statement is too absolute: speakerphone is also allowed if it requires no use of the hands and adequate hearing in both ears is maintained. Holding the phone while riding is not allowed.
On an ordinary two-wheeled moped, the rider must wear an approved, properly fastened helmet while moving. The law provides exemptions for certain vehicles equipped with specific protections.
Caution is necessary on a moped too: keep control and adjust speed to road and traffic conditions.
A moped is a different category from a motorcycle: it is excluded from motorways even though some motorcycles may use them under certain conditions.

Headphones are prohibited even for listening to the radio. They should not be confused with an earpiece for a device, which is allowed only under the conditions for hearing and without using the hands.
The rider of a two-wheeled moped cannot tow another vehicle, even if it has broken down.
A passenger is not always permitted: the seat must be specified on the registration certificate and the rider must be at least 16 years old.
On a two-wheeled moped, you may neither tow nor be towed by another vehicle: the police consider towing a hazardous manoeuvre.
Accelerating gradually helps make a controlled start: sudden acceleration can lift the front wheel and cause loss of control.

During acceleration, load shifts toward the rear wheel, reducing the load on the front wheel; if acceleration is too strong, the front wheel can lift. Accelerating progressively helps keep the start controlled.
Before joining traffic, make sure you will not cause danger or obstruction and yield to vehicles already moving.
Do not start at full speed to get ahead of others: join without causing danger or obstruction and yield to moving vehicles.
Accelerating does not entitle you to ignore priority: when joining traffic, yield to moving vehicles and maneuver without danger.
Do not start with a wheelie: the rider must not travel with the front wheel raised and must keep control.
Slightly bent arms let you steer without stretching them. Legs slightly apart and feet firmly on the footrests help provide stability in the seat.
Sitting so you can reach the handlebars with slightly bent arms allows you to steer without stretching.
When stopped, being able to place your feet firmly on the ground helps support the moped; while moving, keep your feet on the supports.
Do not ride standing on the footboard: sit correctly to control the vehicle.
Sitting too far back with straight arms forces you to stretch to steer. The correct position lets you reach the handlebars with slightly bent arms.
While moving, keep your feet on the supports, near any foot controls, to maintain balance and control.
Even on a clear straight road, watch the road: an obstacle or another hazard may appear suddenly.
A straight road without traffic does not eliminate every hazard: adjust speed to conditions and keep the vehicle under control.
Even when the road is clear, travel on the right-hand side of the carriageway, near its right edge.
Looking at the scenery takes attention away from the road. Even on a clear straight road, watch the carriageway and possible hazards.
Even on a straight road, obstacles or other hazards can appear: stay alert and ready to stop.
On a two-wheeled moped, you must not do a wheelie, even on a straight, empty road: you risk losing control of the vehicle.
Looking ahead helps you spot obstacles and keep control: a greeting must not distract you from the road.
Even without visible traffic, obstacles can appear: keep your attention on riding.
Caution is needed even on a clear straight road: you must be able to control the vehicle and react to foreseeable obstacles.
Turning around to greet someone takes your eyes off the road. Keep looking ahead and maintain control.
Braking too abruptly can cause the wheels to lose grip and lead to a fall, even on an empty road. To stop and greet someone, check that the manoeuvre is safe and signal in good time.
Even when going to meet a friend, check that the change of direction is safe and signal in good time: the signal informs other road users of the manoeuvre you intend to make.
Grip is reduced in the wet: slowing down and using the controls gradually helps prevent skids.
Wet rails and manhole covers can be slippery: spot them early and approach them with care.
Braking sharply in the wet can cause a skid and a fall; braking gradually helps maintain balance.
Avoiding splashing pedestrians shows consideration for other road users: slow down near puddles.
Painted markings can be slippery when wet: braking on them can cause a loss of grip.
Rain calls for a speed suited to reduced grip, not acceleration to cover more ground.
Rain does not always require you to stop: you can continue with adjusted riding if conditions allow safe control.
Increasing speed does not prevent skids: slow down and use the controls gradually in the wet.
Get off and push the moped by hand, walking on its right. At the right edge of the road, this keeps the moped between you and the traffic.
A rider of a two-wheeled moped must not be towed by another vehicle; move the broken-down moped safely.
If the vehicle cannot be moved off the carriageway, place it parallel to the road at the right edge and warn of the hazard.
Do not push the moped while seated on it: get off and push it from the ground. Standing beside it allows you to support it with your body and use the brake to control it as you clear the carriageway.
Removing the plate does not remove the obstruction: clear the carriageway as far as possible and warn of the hazard.
A rider of a two-wheeled moped must not be towed by another vehicle, even another moped.
A door can open into the moped’s path: anticipate this hazard and leave room.
A visor or goggles protect the eyes from wind, which can impair vision and delay detection of hazards.
Flapping clothing can catch on controls or wheels; suitable, close-fitting clothing is preferable.
Suitable clothing should allow free movement and operation of the controls without restriction.
Sandals and slippers leave the feet poorly protected. Sturdy footwear that covers and supports the ankles is preferable.
Flapping clothing can catch on controls or wheels. For visibility, choose bright colors or reflective elements on suitable clothing.
The maximum limit is not a target speed: approaching traffic lights, adapt your speed to traffic and be able to stop safely.
A queue alone does not permit crossing a solid line. If it is paired with a broken line, it may be crossed from the broken-line side, provided the other traffic rules are respected.
Staying calm when others make mistakes helps avoid aggressive reactions and handle the situation attentively.
Watching others and anticipating their possible movements gives you more time to recognize and respond to danger.
Smoking occupies a hand needed to control the handlebars. On a two-wheeled moped, normally hold them with both hands, except when a maneuver or signal requires otherwise.
Headphones do not improve attention: they can distract from riding. The road code prohibits a rider from using them.
An animal cannot travel loose on the footboard: on a two-wheeled moped it must be kept in a suitable, secured cage or container within the prescribed load limits.
Reading billboards takes your eyes off the road. Keep your attention on traffic and hazards that may appear.
In normal road traffic, speed racing is prohibited; organized competitions are subject to specific authorization rules.
Light traffic does not make a speed race on the road lawful: the prohibition also applies on roads outside built-up areas.

For an unlawful speed race involving motor vehicles, conviction entails confiscation of participants’ vehicles, with an exception for an owner unconnected to the offense who did not lend them for that purpose.
Nighttime does not authorize speed racing on the road: the prohibition does not depend on the time.
A limited-traffic zone does not authorize speed races: traffic rules apply there too.
Modifying the engine does not authorize racing on the road. The prohibition on speed racing still applies.
Frequent mirror checks help you monitor the situation behind and choose a safe maneuver, without neglecting what is happening ahead.
Letting a vehicle that is following too closely pass removes that insufficient gap behind you. You can leave the roadway or use a suitable parking area when it is safe to do so.
Letting a vehicle that follows too closely pass, when safe, removes its immediate pressure from behind.
There is no obligation to accelerate: you may simply end up with the vehicle too close at a higher speed. Let it pass when safe.
Braking sharply without need can cause a rear-end collision if the following vehicle is too close. Instead, create space and help it pass.
Gesturing at the following driver can take a hand off the handlebars and distract you. Keep control and facilitate passing when safely possible.
Before lending a moped, check that the person meets the driving requirements: entrusting it to someone without the required license is prohibited.
The exhaust becomes very hot during use and can cause contact burns even after riding. Avoid touching it until it has cooled.
The plate must stay clean and legible so the moped can be identified.
Exhaust gases can build up in an enclosed space: they contain carbon monoxide, a poisonous, odorless gas.

The quiz marks this FALSE: you cannot assume that a helmet makes outside sounds easier to hear. In a road test, there was no significant difference in detection of the test signal; other guidance notes that in some conditions hearing can be as good or better. A helmet must still be worn while riding a moped, except for the specific exemptions for certain vehicles.
A turn must be signaled sufficiently in advance; this duty does not depend on other vehicles passing.
Weaving between lanes to arrive sooner is dangerous. Each lane change requires checking that the maneuver will not endanger or obstruct others and signaling in advance.
From age 14 a person may be criminally liable: for a minor, the capacity to understand and the capacity to exercise their will at the time of the act also matter.
On a two-wheeled moped, objects may not project more than 50 cm sideways from the axis or lengthwise beyond the outline; they must also be secured and not obstruct the view.
The manufacturer’s identification plate identifies the vehicle and must remain attached: removing it is prohibited.
On a two-wheeled moped, packages do not justify riding one-handed: keep your hands free and hold the handlebars with both hands, except when a maneuver or signal requires otherwise.
