Do not ride on the rear wheel alone: raising the front wheel is prohibited even when overtaking.
Riding side by side in the same lane reduces the space available to avoid an obstacle. In a group, keep space between vehicles instead of riding abreast.
Bright colors help other road users distinguish the rider, especially in daylight.
Retroreflective inserts return headlight beams toward their source, making the rider more visible in the dark.
Reflectors return light from headlights: when clean and unobstructed they can make the vehicle easier to recognize.
Better visibility does not require riding in the middle of the road: normally vehicles travel on the right, close to the right edge.
The horn is not for continually announcing your presence: use it sparingly for road safety.
In the dark, dark clothing makes the rider harder to distinguish; reflective inserts help drivers whose lights shine on them see the rider.
An unnecessarily low speed can slow vehicles behind and obstruct traffic; speed must still suit the conditions.
A faster vehicle can rapidly catch up with a slow one, increasing the risk of a rear-end collision if enough distance is not maintained.
Unnecessarily slow travel can prompt following drivers to overtake; attempting this without enough space or visibility is dangerous. The overtaking driver remains responsible for the maneuver.
Traveling too slowly without reason can obstruct following vehicles: the code prohibits obstructing traffic by unjustifiably slow travel.
Low speed does not exempt you from wearing a helmet: while riding a moped, it must be worn properly fastened, except for the specific exemptions for certain vehicles.
Even at low speed, signal a turn sufficiently in advance so others can understand the maneuver.
Even in a group, leave distance from the vehicle ahead so you can stop in time without hitting it.
Avoiding overtaking within the group helps maintain predictable positions and space between riders; an emergency may require a different maneuver.
When riding in a group, it is prudent not to ride side by side, leaving each rider room to maneuver and react.
Riding side by side in the same lane reduces room to maneuver. In a group, it is prudent not to ride abreast.
For two-wheeled mopeds, the ban on being towed also applies when riding in a group: the vehicle ahead cannot pull the one behind.
Riding in a group does not permit exceeding speed limits: each rider must obey them and adjust speed to the conditions.
A different moped may have unfamiliar controls and handling. Get to know it before tackling demanding situations.
Braking response can vary from one vehicle to another: on an unfamiliar moped, you need to become familiar with the effectiveness of its brakes and the force needed.
Mopeds can respond differently to steering. Without knowing how a new vehicle responds, you may misjudge your path through a turn. Get familiar with it in a controlled area.
Practicing in a safe, low-traffic place lets you learn the controls, braking and steering without immediately facing heavy traffic.
The controls of an unfamiliar vehicle can respond differently even before riding. Get familiar with the throttle and brakes without waiting until maximum speed.

Trying a different moped does not exempt the rider from wearing a helmet: while riding, an approved helmet must be worn and fastened. Exemptions apply to three- or four-wheeled mopeds with enclosed bodywork and to two- or three-wheeled mopeds with a crash-resistant safety cell, restraint systems and safety devices as required by the regulations.
Getting familiar with the vehicle does not justify exceeding limits. Mopeds are designed for a maximum speed of no more than 45 km/h; any lower limits also apply.
The normal riding position keeps hands on the handlebars and feet on the supports to control the vehicle and maintain balance. One hand may be temporarily released when needed to maneuver or signal.
A stable position, with hands and feet ready to operate the controls, helps maintain balance and control.
The riding position must allow the rider to sit correctly and maintain control. Standing up while riding compromises this position.
Zigzagging is not a proper way to be noticed. Maintain a steady path and signal necessary maneuvers.
Holding a phone distracts the rider and removes a hand from the controls. Do not use a handheld phone while riding.
Meeting an oncoming moped does not call for sounding the horn. Use it sparingly for road safety, not as a greeting.
If the vehicle ahead is slow to move off, waiting allows time to resume without causing risky maneuvers or unnecessary noise.
The horn is for safety and must be used sparingly; a short delay moving off does not justify repeated honking.
A signal to proceed does not make an improper overtake safe. Before any maneuver, check that it will not endanger or obstruct others.
Repeatedly honking to hurry the driver ahead is improper. Use the horn sparingly for road safety.
Do not make a U-turn at or near an intersection to get around a stopped vehicle. Wait and choose only permitted, safe maneuvers.

Injury or damage to people, animals or property caused by a vehicle in circulation can lead to compensation. Proof that the driver did everything possible to prevent the damage overcomes the presumption against the driver in the first paragraph of article 2054; liability remains, however, for damage caused by construction defects or inadequate maintenance.

The owner need not be present: the owner is jointly liable with the driver. Proof that the vehicle was used against the owner’s will overcomes the liability provided for in the third paragraph of article 2054; liability remains, however, for damage caused by construction defects or inadequate maintenance.

Civil liability is intended to make good the harm suffered by the injured party: the person liable must compensate for it. The law allows the driver to prove that they did everything possible to avoid the damage.
In a collision between vehicles, drivers are presumed to have contributed equally to the damage until proved otherwise. The facts may rebut that presumption.
Civil compensation can cover both property damage and personal injury.
Minor damage does not in itself rule out compensation: there must be compensable damage and the relevant conditions must be met.
The policy limit caps insurance cover; the responsible person bears the excess.
Civil liability concerns compensation for damage; assisting injured people is a separate duty following an accident.
Serious injury negligently caused by a breach of traffic rules can constitute an offence; the conditions for personal liability must be established.
Negligently causing a death can constitute an offence; criminal liability requires its conditions to be established.
Criminal liability requires an act defined by law as an offence and attributable to the person, for example serious road injury caused by negligence.
Criminal liability is personal to the person who committed the offence; it does not automatically transfer to others.
The person who caused the event is criminally liable when all elements of an offence are established; involvement in an accident alone is not enough.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the statement does not specify the conditions for criminal liability. Negligent injury requires fault and the other elements of the offence; minor injuries can also be relevant, so severity alone does not decide liability.
Not every traffic violation is a crime: some carry an administrative penalty. Criminal liability requires the elements of an offence.
Criminal liability is personal: it does not automatically pass to a parent because the driver is a minor.
Helping an injured person is a separate duty and does not automatically erase any criminal liability arising from the accident.
To avoid obstruction, clear the carriageway if possible; if the vehicle cannot be taken off it, place it at the right edge, parallel to the road.
If the moped obstructs the road and cannot be removed, signal the danger with suitable means and inform the road authority or police.
If the moped cannot be removed, calling assistance and waiting helps arrange its removal; meanwhile signal the obstruction and inform the road authority or police.
A sheet does not remove the obstruction. Clear the carriageway as far as possible and signal the danger.
The pavement is not automatically the place for the vehicle: clear the carriageway without creating another danger or obstruction.
A report to the nearest police station is not required in every case: stop, make the area safe and communicate useful details to the affected party.
Even if the owner is absent, communicate your identity and other information useful for compensation to them by available means.
Make your identity and useful information available to the affected party, seeking the owner of the vehicle hit.
Damage to another person’s vehicle must be compensated when the conditions for civil liability are met, even if it was parked.
The absence of witnesses does not remove the duties: stop and make your details available to the affected party even when they are absent.
Being a minor does not automatically remove liability for damage: the minor’s capacity and, under the legal conditions, parental liability matter.
After the collision, stop and give your details to the person whose vehicle was damaged, using an available means if they are absent. Fear of blame does not justify leaving.
Even when only property is damaged, the driver involved must stop, check the situation and give the affected party the relevant details.
Staying calm helps you assess the situation, warn of hazards and provide the necessary information accurately.
You cannot leave immediately: even without injuries, you must stop and give your details. You can notify your parents without neglecting these duties.
Being a minor does not remove the duty to stop and provide details after an accident connected with your conduct.
Warning approaching traffic helps prevent vehicles entering the danger area and causing another accident. Give the warning without exposing yourself to further danger.
Oil on the road creates a hazard for approaching traffic. Warn others and protect traffic safety.
Warning of the danger helps prevent other vehicles from hitting the injured person who cannot be moved.
Warn of danger whenever the situation requires it, even without fog: vehicles or people in the road can surprise approaching drivers.
There is no need to wait for traffic to stop: an obstacle or person in the road can be dangerous even while vehicles are still moving.
Street lighting in a built-up area does not necessarily remove the danger. Warn approaching traffic there too if the situation requires it.
If people are injured, call 112 and describe the location and situation: this information helps get the necessary services, including the police when needed.
If people are injured, call 112 and describe the location and situation: this information helps get the necessary services, including the police when needed.
If the other driver cannot demonstrate insurance coverage, call the police to investigate. Failure to demonstrate coverage alone does not prove it is absent.
Vehicle damage is not the only reason to call the police: their attendance may also be necessary when people are injured.
The absence of witnesses alone does not make a police call mandatory. The circumstances matter, such as whether anyone is injured.
The emergency dispatcher needs to know where the accident is, how many people are involved and their condition, so appropriate help can be arranged.
Contact emergency services promptly: call 112 and describe the situation. 118 is medical emergency assistance and 113 is the police.
118 activates medical emergency assistance for accidents involving people in danger; you can also call 112 and describe the location and situation.
Do not give food or drink to a traumatized person, including alcohol. Call emergency services and follow their instructions.
Do not continue on and ignore injured people: stop, call emergency services and provide whatever assistance you can.
The duty to help does not depend on responsibility: someone who finds an injured person must provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Before intervening, assess hazards at the scene and warn others, so the rescuer and other people do not become victims too.

Call emergency services and remain safely at the scene to protect injured people, following the operator’s instructions. When the police officers arrive, you can give them useful information about what happened.
Safely warning others about the accident with the means available alerts approaching traffic and reduces the risk of further collisions.
Do not leave the scene without helping: call emergency services and assist the person safely, following the dispatcher's instructions.
Knowing the injured person's name is not a condition for helping: call emergency services and report the location and the person's condition as far as you know them.
The helper must not give medication: call emergency services and follow the dispatcher's instructions.
Helping an injured person is a duty of solidarity as well as a legal obligation: immediately notifying the authorities is also a form of help provided for by law.
Article 593 of the Criminal Code requires someone who finds an injured person to provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Assistance and a prompt emergency call can prevent deterioration and help the person receive timely care; the law requires necessary assistance or immediate notification of the authorities.
Providing help is mandatory: someone who finds an injured person must provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
The duty is not limited to healthcare professionals: anyone who finds an injured person must provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Fear of becoming involved does not remove the duty: someone who finds an injured person must provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Alcohol can reduce inhibitions and risk perception and cause excitement, so the driver may act recklessly.
Alcohol can slow reflexes and reactions, making it harder to recognize and respond to danger while driving.
Alcohol can cause drowsiness, reducing the alertness needed to follow the road.
Alcohol can reduce attention and control, making it harder to concentrate on driving situations.
Alcohol can reduce alertness and attention, making it harder to notice what is happening on the road in time.
Alcohol does not eliminate tiredness: it can instead cause drowsiness and reduce alertness.
Alcohol does not improve concentration: it can reduce the attention and control needed to drive.
Alcohol does not make people more alert or attentive: it can reduce alertness and attention even when they feel less inhibited.
Feeling less inhibited does not make driving better: alcohol can reduce risk perception and encourage reckless behavior.
Alcohol does not improve vision: it can reduce peripheral vision and make it harder to notice what happens to the sides.
Intoxication impairs attention, judgment and reflexes: the driver may fail to recognize or respond in time to a danger to themselves and others.
Driving while intoxicated is prohibited. Penalties vary with blood alcohol level: the higher ranges carry both a fine and arrest, while the lower range carries an administrative penalty.
Police may measure alcohol levels with suitable instruments in the cases provided for; refusal of the test is punishable by law.
The ban on driving while intoxicated applies every day, not just at weekends.
The ban on driving while intoxicated also applies without passengers: their absence does not eliminate the danger to traffic.
Driving at a moderate speed does not permit driving while intoxicated: the ban still applies.
Drugs can alter perception and slow reactions, making it harder to recognize and respond to danger.
The effects depend on the substance: some cause drowsiness, others excitement; both can impair driving.
A substance can slow reactions and impair coordination, making the vehicle harder to control.
Drugs do not make driving safer: they can impair judgment, perception and reaction time.
Drugs do not necessarily improve self-control: they can impair judgment and encourage risky behavior.
Drugs do not necessarily improve vision: cannabis, for example, can impair judgment of distance.
Alcohol can reduce attention and judgment, making it harder to recognize danger and react in time.
Drugs can impair attention and judgment, making danger harder for the driver to recognize.
Sleeping pills can cause drowsiness and impair attention and judgment, even when the driver does not realize the risk.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Caffeine in energy drinks can temporarily increase alertness, but effects depend on the amount and the person: it can disturb sleep and does not replace rest. Do not drive when sleepy.

The quiz marks this FALSE. In ordinary culinary use, spices differ from the intoxicating substances discussed in the nearby questions. This does not apply to excessive doses: large amounts of nutmeg, for example, can cause severe drowsiness.

The quiz marks this FALSE. An ordinary non-alcoholic fizzy drink differs from an alcoholic drink: carbonation itself does not cause alcohol intoxication. Drinks can have different ingredients and effects; drinking while driving can distract you.
The prohibition also protects road structures and installations: damaging them can endanger traffic.
Nothing may be thrown from a moving vehicle: it can dirty the road or create a hazard.
It is forbidden to deposit waste on the road or its associated areas, which must remain clear and clean.
Giving way to pedestrians is not forbidden: for example, at an uncontrolled crossing drivers must slow down and stop for people crossing or immediately nearby.
The horn is not forbidden everywhere: use it sparingly for safety; in built-up areas it is allowed in actual and immediate danger.
There is no general prohibition: mopeds must use lights even during the day; daytime running lights may replace dipped headlights where permitted.
A steady speed, when conditions permit, avoids unnecessary acceleration and braking that increase fuel consumption.
Frequent or harsh acceleration uses more fuel; smooth driving helps reduce consumption.
Maintenance according to the manufacturer’s instructions helps limit waste: for example, repairing an out-of-tune engine can reduce fuel consumption, with results varying by repair.
High speed is not a way to save fuel: air resistance increases with speed and fuel consumption can rise.
There is no need to avoid level roads: climbing requires extra energy, and the fuel saved downhill does not always offset the fuel used uphill.
During a prolonged stop, a running engine consumes fuel without moving; switching it off avoids this waste.
Keeping the fuel system in good condition helps limit emissions: for example, on a carbureted moped, correct carburetor adjustment forms part of exhaust emissions control.
Maintaining the ignition system, including the spark plugs, helps prevent misfires that can increase hydrocarbon emissions.
The air filter should be maintained and replaced on the manufacturer’s schedule. In carbureted engines, a clogged filter can reduce the air in the mixture and increase carbon monoxide emissions.
Do not lower the pressure: underinflated tires increase resistance and fuel consumption. Maintain the pressure specified by the manufacturer.
The limit is the maximum permitted speed, not a target: high speeds can increase fuel consumption and emissions.
Revving repeatedly while stationary consumes fuel and produces emissions without moving the vehicle; it does not reduce pollution.
Using less fuel reduces the amount burned and can therefore reduce emissions from combustion.
A steady speed suited to traffic avoids unnecessary acceleration and braking that increase fuel use and emissions.
During a prolonged stop, switching off the engine prevents it from needlessly burning fuel and emitting gases while stationary.
Constantly running the engine at maximum rpm needlessly increases fuel consumption. Avoid unnecessarily high engine speeds.
Revving while stopped wastes fuel and produces unnecessary emissions. During a prolonged stop the engine can be switched off.
Revving on the stand burns fuel without covering any distance and produces emissions: it does not reduce pollution.
The silencer reduces exhaust noise: it must be kept in working order and be an approved type for the vehicle.
In built-up areas the horn is normally prohibited and may be used in actual and immediate danger. In case of necessity, an exception applies to vehicles carrying seriously injured or ill people.
Skidding tires make noise. Avoid unnecessary hard braking, while remaining ready to brake firmly when safety requires it.
The horn is for road safety, not for reprimanding a driver who has committed an offense. Use it sparingly and only for safety.
Spinning the tires when starting creates nuisance noise. At green, move off without spinning them and respect the conditions at the intersection.
Repeatedly revving during a stop creates unnecessary noise; it does not help traffic flow.
An efficient silencer approved for the vehicle reduces exhaust noise; its condition should be checked.
A damaged exhaust must be replaced with one approved for that vehicle to restore adequate noise reduction.
Unusual brake noise should be checked: an inspection can identify component problems and address the cause of the squeal.
Modifying the silencer to increase performance is not a way to reduce noise: it must remain effective and conform to the approved type.
Removing the exhaust silencer removes its noise reduction. The vehicle must have an effective silencer.
Just any silencer is not enough: the replacement must be approved for the vehicle and work properly.
When the siren and blue light are operating, leave a clear passage for the emergency vehicle and stop if necessary.
The siren signals a vehicle on an urgent service: leave its passage clear and stop if necessary. Pulling over to the right and stopping can help it pass.
The vehicle is performing an urgent service: a clear passage helps it reach its destination quickly. Stop if necessary.
Do not drive onto the sidewalk: leave the way clear and stop if necessary, without entering the space used by pedestrians.
Do not follow an emergency vehicle closely to take advantage of the gap it creates; leave its passage clear.
The duty to leave the way clear applies to everyone on the road concerned, not just bulky vehicles; stop if necessary.

On a two-wheeled moped, both towing and being towed are prohibited. The weight being towed can make the vehicle less stable and reduce braking effectiveness; when the moped is being towed, the force of the connection can impair steering and control.

Avoiding a lying-forward position helps you keep a posture from which you can watch the road and use your arms to steer rather than just support yourself. Reducing air resistance must not compromise control.
Loss or theft of the plate must be reported to the police within 48 hours; contact the vehicle licensing office for a new plate.

Not always: the procedure for a transported third party does not apply if the crash was caused by a fortuitous event. In other cases, the insurer of the vehicle the passenger was in compensates them up to the statutory minimum coverage limit, subject to the rules for multiple affected parties when the damage exceeds the coverage limit. For additional damage, a claim can still be made against the liable party’s insurer if its coverage limit is higher.
A moped cannot carry two passengers: only one passenger may be carried if the seat is listed on the registration certificate and the rider meets the age requirement.
The insurance disc no longer needs to be displayed. Insurance remains compulsory and the insurance certificate must be available on board.

Claustrophobia does not exempt anyone from wearing an approved helmet correctly fastened. There is, however, an exception for two-wheeled mopeds equipped with a crash-tested safety cell and the prescribed restraint systems and safety devices.
If the road does not allow a slow vehicle to be overtaken easily and safely, slow down and, if necessary, pull aside as soon as possible to let others pass.
When a slow vehicle cannot be overtaken easily and safely, slow down and, if necessary, pull aside as soon as possible to let following traffic pass.
If the road makes overtaking a slow vehicle difficult or dangerous, slow down and, if necessary, pull aside safely as soon as possible.
Moving to the center does not help others overtake. If the road makes overtaking a slow vehicle difficult or dangerous, slow down and, if necessary, pull aside as soon as possible.
A U-turn is not the required maneuver. If overtaking a slow vehicle is difficult or dangerous, slow down and, if necessary, pull aside as soon as possible.
The left indicator is not an invitation to overtake: it signals a maneuver to the left. If necessary, the slow vehicle pulls aside as soon as possible to let others pass.
Having priority does not remove the duty to avoid a collision: if the other road user does not stop, brake and let them pass when necessary.
Having priority does not prevent a collision if another road user fails to give way. You must therefore do what you can to avoid it, stopping if necessary.
The horn does not authorize you to go first regardless: reduce speed and stop if necessary to avoid a collision.
Care is always needed at a junction; when it is our turn to give way, we must also let the other road users pass.
Liability does not automatically rest solely with the person who failed to give way: the conduct of the other drivers is also assessed.
A green light does not authorize blocking the junction: if traffic prevents you from clearing it, wait before entering.
The traffic officer’s signals take precedence over the traffic light: obey a signal to stop even when the light is green.
On hearing an emergency vehicle’s siren, leave its way clear and stop if necessary: a green light does not permit obstructing it.
The green light takes precedence over the give-way sign: the sign alone does not require you to stop. You must still obey the other rules when crossing.
The green light takes precedence over the STOP sign: the sign alone does not require you to stop. You must still obey the other rules when crossing.
A vehicle’s flashing amber light warns of danger but does not automatically give it priority. With a green light you may proceed while obeying the other traffic rules.
A mirror does not show the entire area around the moped: a vehicle or pedestrian may be outside its field of view. Check the blind spot too before changing position.
A working mirror lets you observe traffic behind; a damaged or faulty one can make the view unreliable.
A securely mounted mirror stays in position and, adjusted from the normal riding position, provides a useful view behind and to the side.
Dirt and cracks can impair the view: cleaning the mirror and replacing it if damaged helps you see clearly behind.
Mirrors must be of an approved type suitable for the vehicle: an unapproved device has not undergone the same verification of the prescribed requirements.
The load must leave lights, signals and the number plate visible so others can see the signals and identify the vehicle.
The rider must be able to move their arms, hands and legs freely: a load that obstructs the controls prevents proper control of the moped.
A moped leans in a bend: a load that is too low can touch the ground and impair stability. Place it with sufficient ground clearance.
An unsecured load can shift or fall, affecting stability or endangering others. It must be firmly secured.
A load that projects too far can affect handling and stability. Two-wheeled mopeds also have projection limits measured from the centreline and outline.
On a two-wheeled moped the load may project longitudinally at most 50 cm beyond the vehicle outline, not 80 cm.

For a two-wheeled moped, the lateral limit is 50 cm from the vehicle’s axis, not a maximum of 30 cm. A 30 cm projection is within that dimensional limit, provided the load is securely fastened and does not restrict visibility.
The load need not be attached to the handlebars, mudguards and fork. It must instead be firmly secured without restricting the movements needed to ride.
Fatigue can temporarily reduce physical and mental performance: attention, judgment and reaction ability deteriorate while riding.
Fatigue can be accompanied by drowsiness, making it difficult to stay alert and even leading to brief episodes of sleep.
Fatigue can reduce concentration and impair vision, making it harder to spot a hazard in time.
Fatigue can impair judgment and vision, causing errors in judging distances and available space.
Fatigue is a serious danger: it can slow reactions, reduce attention and lead to sleep while riding.
Fatigue can occur during the day too, for example after too little sleep or prolonged driving; it is not limited to night.
Fatigue slows reactions rather than speeding them up and can delay recognition of a hazard.
Drowsiness reduces alertness and can lead to brief involuntary sleep: the rider loses awareness and control of their actions.
Fatigue promotes drowsiness: as tiredness increases, staying alert becomes harder.
Drowsiness reduces alertness and can weaken your perception of speed, making it harder to judge how fast you are travelling and react in time.
Drowsiness reduces alertness and the ability to concentrate on driving, rather than increasing them.
Drowsiness impairs alertness and control of speed and direction; it does not improve moped control.
The quiz marks this FALSE: monotony and lack of sleep can promote drowsiness. A demanding route does not rule it out, however: if you are sleepy, stop safely and rest.
A substance can impair judgment and reaction time even after one use, encouraging reckless driving.
Effects depend on the substance and dose: even one use can cause confusion and impair driving for several hours.
Some substances can temporarily distort perception, making it harder to assess what is happening on the road.
Even one use can impair the attention needed to follow the road and react to unexpected events.
Drugs can impair judgment, not improve it. Feeling confident does not mean being capable of driving safely.
The driving danger comes from the substance’s effects on the driver’s abilities. Use alone does not automatically lead to vehicle confiscation; driving after use can have separate legal consequences.
The risk comes from the substance’s effects on driving, not automatic administrative impoundment for use alone. Driving after use can have separate legal consequences.
Alcohol and sleeping pills can combine their sedative effects, increasing drowsiness and difficulty concentrating.
Alcohol and certain painkillers or sedatives can increase each other’s sedative effects; the interaction depends on the medicine.
On an empty stomach alcohol is absorbed faster and can reach a higher blood concentration than after a meal.
A glass of cold water is not what amplifies alcohol’s effect; alcohol already consumed nevertheless continues to be absorbed and impair driving.
Drinking slowly does not itself amplify alcohol’s effects. Alcohol consumed can still impair judgment and coordination.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the combined effects of alcohol and nicotine cannot be summed up for every person and situation. Alcohol impairs driving: smoking a cigarette does not make it safe to drive after drinking.
Used engine oil must be collected and passed to the authorized collection system; a private individual can also take it to an equipped municipal collection center.
Used oil is waste to be collected separately: pouring it down a drain can pollute and is no substitute for taking it to a suitable collection center.
Used oil can contaminate the environment: collect it and take it to a suitable collection point, rather than releasing it into soil or water.
Solvent does not make it lawful to pour used oil into the sewer. Collect the oil separately without mixing it with other substances.
Do not burn used oil yourself: hand it to an authorized collector for appropriate treatment.
Do not add water to used oil: the mixture hinders recovery. Take the oil separately to a suitable collection point.
Objects can obstruct or endanger traffic. If they can be removed without exposure to vehicles, clear the road; otherwise signal the danger.
Notifying the road operator or maintenance staff allows the hazard to be addressed; if necessary, warn other road users too.
A wheel passing over objects or uneven ground can become unstable; on two wheels this can cause a fall.
Do not ignore the danger: try to clear the road promptly if possible without putting yourself at risk. Also warn other road users of the obstruction and inform the road authority or police.
Do not wait until night: try to remove the obstruction promptly if possible without putting yourself at risk. Also warn other road users of the danger and inform the road authority or police.
Moving objects towards the centre can obstruct or endanger traffic. Instead, clear the road as far as possible and warn others of the danger.
Notifying the road manager allows action to be taken: the road authority is responsible for road maintenance and inspections.
A collapsed surface or open manhole can surprise approaching users; warning them helps make them aware of the danger.
Slowing down gives more room to control the vehicle and stop before a foreseeable hazard.
Do not automatically enter the oncoming lane: slow down and stop if you cannot get around the hazard safely.
Do not climb into the manhole: it may be a dangerous confined space. Report the problem to the road manager.
A collapse or open manhole should be reported because it endangers traffic, whatever service the manhole belongs to.
